utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. This is Tuesday, and I greet Mr. Stojic, Mr. Petkovic and Mr. Pusic, as well as Defence counsels, our witness, Mr. Praljak, and I also greet Mr. Mundis [as interpreted] and all his assistants. And I'm also greeting everyone helping us. I apologise. It is Mr. Stringer, not Mr. Mundis. I apologise. It's Mr. Stringer, representing the OTP. I will give the floor to our Registrar for a couple of numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. 2D has submitted its objections to documents tendered by the Prosecution through Witness Dragan Juric. This list shall be given Exhibit IC1002. And the Prosecution has also submitted its objections to documents tendered by 2D through Witness Dragan Juric. This list shall be given Exhibit IC1003. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. Let me first issue an oral decision. It's quite short. Oral decision on the Stojic Defence motion to reconsider the oral decision made on April 7, 2009. On April 14th, 2009, the Stojic Defence filed a motion to reconsider the oral decision made on the 7th of April, 2009, in which the Trial Chamber rejected the fact that Exhibit 2D01532 would be added on list 65 ter of the Stojic Defence.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, it's 2D01533.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In its motion, the Stojic Defence submits that Exhibit 2D01533 is a crucial document for the Stojic Defence case and also submits that postponing Witness Drago Juric, who had been planned to testify from April 6th and 7, 2009, to April 27 and 28, 2009, is a new fact that would require the oral decision of April 7, 2009, to be reconsidered. The Trial Chamber notes that the Prosecution and the other Defence teams filed no answer to this request made by the Stojic Defence. The Trial Chamber recalls that in its oral decision of April 7th, 2009, it had, inter alia, given the grounds to reject adding Exhibit 2D01533 on the Stojic Defence's 65 ter list by the following fact: It deemed that it had heard enough evidence on the topic that was expounded in Exhibit 2D01533. The Trial Chamber deems that the Stojic Defence did not demonstrate that the reasoning in the impugned decision showed a mistake, and because of this there is no need to reconsider the decision of April 7th, 2009. The Trial Chamber thus decides to dismiss the request made by the Stojic Defence. Mr. Praljak, on behalf of the Trial Chamber, let me tell you that we heard you yesterday, we heard your 84 bis statement, and we also listened to you while you were answering the questions put to you by your counsel. We note that your answers are sometimes extremely lengthy. Therefore, we invite you to be more concise in your answers, to be more to the point, and to answer the question more accurately, because as you may know or as you may not know, everything you say is on the transcript, is in the transcript, and when Judges will deliberate, they will refer to the transcript. In the trial judgement, there will be, I'm sure, many footnotes that will refer to the transcript. So if you start expounding on a subject at length, this might be considered as a waste of time for your case. So please try and be very specific and very concise in your answers. Don't forget that everything you say might have probative value. You are under oath, of course, so this by definition means you're telling the truth. Everything you say is of utmost importance, but try not to water down your evidence by being too lengthy, because we might lose track of the essentials. I wanted to remind you of this in order for your defence to be as effective as possible and for you not to waste any time. I have a couple of questions to ask, following the answers that you gave us yesterday. Short questions, but usually I spend the entire night thinking about what has been said during the day in order to revisit the issue, if need be, and here I really believe that it is important to revisit this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yesterday, you told us you did not do your service in the JNA because you had a hip problem. You also told us that you were wounded in a leg in Syria. Could you tell us exactly how you were wounded in Syria? What were the circumstances?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, after being in the Yugoslav People's Army for three months and then dismissed from the army due to incapacity, I have a leg injury, an ankle injury, actually, not a hip injury. I said my ankle was injured, and that's why I had the nickname that I had, as I told you. And it was a cart in Tomislavgrad, while I was a child, that the wheel went over my leg, and it was a cart carrying stones. It wasn't in Syria, no. I've never been to Syria. That's quite wrong. Not Syria. So this injury occurred in Tomislavgrad when I was a child. A horse and cart drove over my leg, and so I didn't spend more than three months in the Yugoslav People's Army. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Second question now. Yesterday, I was listening to you with great interest, when you started talking about the history of your country and when you talked about the partisans and Ante Pavelic. Everything you said was extremely interesting, and one could conclude from this that during this troubled time in Croatia, in the history of Croatia, there was, in Croatia, people who had become partisans, probably under the aegis of the late Marshal Tito, and others had joined the ranks of Ante Pavelic's units and were members of the Ustasha movement. This was very interesting, and I understood, but maybe I made a mistake, so correct me if I'm wrong. I understood that after 1945, the partisans took power with Marshal Tito, and at the level of the Republic of Croatia and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia these people were in positions of power. So you know, and this is no secret, that in the indictment and in the preliminary brief, the notion of JCE, joint criminal enterprise, can also involve this Ustasha phenomenon, who according to the Prosecutor these Ustasha would have wanted -- these people would have wanted to recreate the Greater Croatia. Now this is why I want to come back to what you said, because this is something that was very important. You talked about General Bobetko. You know as well as I do that General Bobetko is a member of the JCE. It's in the indictment. But yesterday you added that General Bobetko was a former partisan, so logically I could infer from this that since Bobetko was a partisan, he had nothing to do with the followers of Ante Pavelic. Normally, he was on the other side and he was fighting against those people. You were a person of importance at the time, so could you confirm that General Bobetko was indeed a former partisan and that he did not accept the ideas of Ante Pavelic's movement? I mean, you knew this person, Bobetko. I've only seen his name, but I've had no inkling of his existence beforehand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Your Honour, Your Honours, first of all, let me put you right. The number of partisans in World War II was far greater, as an anti-fascist movement, from the number of Communists, especially after 1943, who led the movement. So in 1945, all the positions, political posts, military posts, posts in the economy, were occupied by Communists. The Communists had come to power. General Bobetko, not only was he a partisan, but he was the first partisan in Europe, the Sisak Battalion -- Detachment that he established was the first unit that was established in the soil of Europe, standing up to the Hitler coalition. He was a foremost fighter. He was an anti-fascist throughout the war, throughout the whole of the war. Afterwards, he became a general of the Yugoslav People's Army and was a general until 1972, when, within the frameworks of the political movement in Croatia, which was called "The Croatian Spring," he advocated greater independence for Croatia and was then made to retire. So he became active again when the aggression against Croatia was launched, and for a time, for quite some time he was first commander of the Southern Front and then Chief of the Main Staff of the Croatian Army. The first chief of the Croatian Army, General Spegelj, was also a partisan and a general of the Yugoslav People's Army, who had commanded before that the 5th Army Aerial with its centre in Zagreb, and General Tus also came from the Yugoslav People's Army, where before that he was the Chief of Staff for the air force, and he replaced General Spiegel as chief of the Croatia Army, and then General Bobetko came. Franjo Tudjman was also since 1941 an active partisan, and he was a general of the Yugoslav People's Army. He worked in Belgrade for many years and, after that, devoted himself to work as a historian. And in opposing -- well, he was in prison twice, found guilty after 1971, for questioning the number of victims in Jasenovac. And I'd like to tell you that most of the Croatian Government and top Croatian army leaders were in fact people who had been partisans.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'd like to intervene. In the transcript, I think that this is indispensable for understanding because in page 7 the name is lacking, and General Praljak was referring to Franjo Tudjman. Line 1 of page 7; isn't that right, Mr. Praljak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Dr. Tudjman was in the partisan movement from 1941 to 1945. He held senior posts in the partisan movement in norther Croatia, that is to say around Zagreb; and after that was he was in the Yugoslav People's Army and he was a general in the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. One last question. It will be very short. Yesterday, you talked about your father, and we know that he worked in the State security system, and I thought I understood, but I would like you to confirm this. I thought I understood that your father was in favour of maintaining Yugoslavia as it was, so your father seemed to be in favour of the Communist system, at the time he was in favour of Yugoslavia; and I thought I understood, but correct me if I'm wrong; but politically you grew apart from your father because you were not in favour of former Yugoslavia, and you were certainly not in favour of Communism. Is this how I am supposed to understand what you told us yesterday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you understood everything I said quite correctly, but one should bear in mind just one point, Your Honours, and it is this: that people in the Communist movement matured, and there was a debate whether Yugoslavia was necessary or not and what the powers that be should be. This came gradually. It wasn't precipitous. All the people that I mentioned were, first of all, partisans and Communists, hard-line Communists, but as time went by and as the powers that be did some bad things, they came to understand slowly that a state of that kind, in fact, represented stifling the people who belonged to it; and let's call it a democratic system, and that's what happened to my father in 1971, 1972, and later on. People who were ready to lay down their lives for those ideals found it a difficult process, so this happened bit by bit. And, in fact, it was more the people who were in the partisans formerly that began to question the system and movement and began to think otherwise, more so than perhaps young people who would join later on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you for answering these questions. Let me now give the floor to your counsel, and he will resume his examination-in-chief. He did use up about an hour yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Good afternoon to everybody in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, General Praljak, you were talking about the media, and you said that you worked in television and the newspapers of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and you said that Radio Mostar existed in 1992, it was operating and functional. And with respect to the attack on the HVO in 1993, I would like to ask you whether anything changed or, rather, with respect to that date and the events after that date, whether you, yourself, knew at the time that military targets, such as Radio Mostar, were legitimate targets, and similar facilities that you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. Sorry for the interruption. Could we, for the record, specify perhaps more clearly the date of the attack that counsel is referring to, whether it's perhaps May 1993, or June 1993, or another time in 1993?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. I said, "May 9, 1993." I think it was a transcript question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Without any wish to meddle in an interpretation of war law, I'm not a specialist in that, but I nevertheless would like to say that the IPD of the Croatian Army that I headed from 1992 onwards, when in fact the organisation was set up, constantly organised seminars in which all levels of the Croatian Army were spoken to about war law, and war law was interpreted for them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, the President has recalled that you should answer questions and not go into giving lectures of any kind. The question was whether anything changed after 9 May 1993 with regard to Radio Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in my question, I expressly asked Mr. Praljak what he knew about what the legitimate targets were, military targets, and then as an example I said "Radio Mostar." So what his knowledge was about law in that respect at that time. And Mr. Praljak began his answer, the circumstances in which he learnt about that. So I think it's a legitimate question. It's mens rea. It's what he knew as a commander, and he started answering and telling us how he came to know about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Okay, we'll listen to the answer. Please proceed, Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Trechsel, I'll do my best to be as brief as possible, but it's difficult because I have to say what I knew; and I knew about international war law because part of the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Croatia, which I headed, dealt with that subject; and so did I by organising a series of meetings, lectures. I published brochures about international war law together with the Red Cross, and I knew that international war law allowed the bombing or neutralisation of telecommunications systems, communications systems, and radio facilities on the opposite side. And after the 9th of May, 1993, it is true that Radio Mostar, as it was called, which was on the east bank -- in fact, in actual fact, Radio Mostar of the 4th Corps of the BH Army at that time, because it kept broadcasting, but despite the fact that we knew where its location was, not a single artillery shell was fired at it. So that would be my answer.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. With the trial's permission, I'd like to move on to another area now, and that is the question of the shelling of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: General Praljak, would you please tell us what you know and what you feel is important, as an introduction to that topic, and later on we'll carry on discussing the topic through questions and answers.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let's list the main points first. I claim that the Yugoslav People's Army, and later on the Army of Republika Srpska in 1992, in March, April, May, June and onwards, destroyed Mostar, as we were able to see it on the photographs shown here, and especially in the book "Urbicide" which has been provided to this Tribunal, and I also claim that in September/October 1992, I personally toured almost the whole of Mostar and personally saw for myself what had happened and what the destruction of Mostar actually entailed. During the destruction of Mostar, I was in Mostar myself for most of the time. I was there personally. Furthermore, in the autumn of 1992, I sent two individuals from Croatia, one of them was Goran Pavelic and the other one was Goran Mecava. One was a worker of the IPD. The other one dealt in films and was a cameraman, and he had a professional 60-millimetre camera. He was a cameraman. He had the Arrow-Flex camera, and from 1.000 metres with a Kodak colour negative, and I sent them to film the destruction of Mostar, and that's what they did. They completed the task, and the material is now to be found stored in Television Zagreb. It was transferred to a positive and on videotape, so the Ministry of Defence has a copy of the tape and I do too. I have it at home. Now, unfortunately at that time, the time when Mostar was destroyed, in Mostar there were no international observers, except for maybe a few people who left. The international observers arrived in greater numbers afterwards, when the conflict between the BH Army and HVO had already started, and then they were able to see there was shooting on both sides and that Mostar had been destroyed. And from that, they concluded that it was the HVO which had destroyed Mostar. Now, in the fighting between the HVO and the BH Army, buildings were destroyed only at the separation line, that is to say, along the boulevard, the Spanish Square, and Santiceva Street. Luckily, as far as my positions are concerned or the HVO positions, during the conflict between the BH Army and the HVO on the east bank, for 24 hours there were members of the Spanish Battalion who spent time there, and they went around counting the shells falling on the left and right bank; that is to say, on both sides of the line. And from their reports, which the Prosecutor has placed at the disposal of this Trial Chamber, I precisely calculated just how many shells fell on the east bank of Mostar. That piece of paper has been handed over to the Court, and it is an exhibit; and I hope that the Prosecutor, if it should happen to find different figures, will put that right; but there were some 800-odd shells. And I claim that during the conflict and before, when there was no conflict, that both the east bank and west bank of Mostar was shelled by the artillery of the Army of Republika Srpska, more or less, to a greater or lesser extent. And I also claim, to the best of my knowledge, that of the number that I have stated over those five or six months fired from HVO positions to the east side, it's not only the east bank but the whole of the eastern area around Mostar, that at least 25 percent or 30 percent fell from the Serb positions so that they could keep the conflict alive. And then once I would say, There you are, the BH Army is shooting at us, and then the other side would say -- the BH Army would say, Here we have the HVO shooting at us; and that's what would happen, all this shooting to and fro. I also claim that the number of about 600 projectiles over a period of five or six months that were directed at exclusively military facilities on the east bank, in the military sense, were at the level of an attack that would be launched by a battalion, so it's a negligible number for us to be able to talk about any kind of bombing for Mostar, the bombing of Mostar. What the Chamber is looking at here is a table showing how many artillery shells must be fired according to the rules of any army in the world in order to neutralise 25 percent or 50 percent of the enemy forces, and so on and so forth; 5.000, 6.000, those are the figures that we're looking at. The Chamber has that. If need be, I can explain that more.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me. Sorry for the interruption. I may have missed the reference, but I see the general is referring to the binder that he was using yesterday, and there was a reference to a chart. And if we're on one of the tabs, I'm just wondering if counsel could indicate which of the tabs the general is referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, what is this chart? What is the reference?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a table or a chart that I showed here in this courtroom. No, I don't have it here. What I'm saying is it has been shown. The Trial Chamber here has been shown this chart or table. These are NATO charts or tables containing information about how many shells and artillery weapons must fire over a square kilometre in order to neutralise, say, 25 percent or 50 percent or 75 percent of enemy forces. That's the chart I have in mind. Of course, I don't have it in front of me, but I have it in another binder that is in my possession. As far as I remember, it has been made an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. From glancing over, Mr. President, I think we're at tab 5 that the Prosecution at least has. And if I could, with respect, while I'm on my feet, as was the case yesterday, the general is referring and basically testifying on the basis of papers that are contained in the binder, and I think that -- and we've had a number of cases throughout the trial in which witnesses are testifying with notes or with pre-prepared materials, and it's not clear to us, and I think it may be useful to -- I'd like to know the status, if I may, of these notes. Are they going to be tendered into evidence? Are these materials prepared by the general with his counsel? It seems that we're not really getting live testimony so much as reading back of something that's been prepared previously by the general and possibly his counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: If I may assist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic, yesterday, in the 84 bis statement, Mr. Praljak relied on documents that were under tabs. Are you going to seek to tender such documents? That is the question raised, and rightly raised by Mr. Stringer. Could you enlighten us on this, because he saw Mr. Praljak looking at documents and he's of the view that these are documents arising from the statement or other documents that you might seek to tender later on by submitting them to Mr. Praljak. Could you shed some light on this?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, of course I'm only too glad to be given an opportunity to explain this. Nevertheless, there is a number of details involved that I think might be helpful in avoiding any further misunderstandings. First of all, perhaps the detail raised by my learned friend, the last three minutes of General Praljak's answer, in which he mentioned two documents that were used and shown in this courtroom before. He is referring to specific exhibits. We don't have the numbers at our finger-tips or in front of us right now, but I think we all know which ones we're talking about. These have been admitted. General Praljak simply added up some information gleaned from all the SpaBat reports in order to arrive at the total number of shells, and this is something he's just explained. The other document involved was another chart showing artillery information according to NATO standards, the amount of ammunition used up for certain targets. These are military standards. I think Mr. Petkovic helped a little with that. THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may, there is a mistake here. These are expenditure norms of the JNA and not NATO. I think Mr. Kovacic misspoke. Let me just put him right on this. These are expenditure norms prescribed by the JNA, not NATO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thank the general. He's quite correct. I had come across the reference to this being about NATO standards, but after the break we can provide the exact reference for these. As for the question just posed by the Trial Chamber, and then following the question by my learned friend from the OTP, General Praljak prepared his opening statement assuming that he would be given three hours to present his statement, as we had requested. He prepared the statement on his own, unaided, based on any documents in his possession, based on any documents in the Defence team's possession - he doesn't have everything in the Detention Unit - and based on everything that had gone on in this courtroom. You then restricted the time he was allowed, and we decided to take over some of these individual topics for purely practical reasons, practical reasons, since all of this is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, Mr. Kovacic. I'll give you the floor in a moment, but there is a question to be raised straight away. Yesterday, when General Praljak made his statement, we followed the statement based on the binder he gave us, and we could see that he was reading parts of the documents that was in the binder. You told us that that was his own work. Our question is as follows: Was the binder given yesterday to the Prosecution? Did the Prosecution receive it? You say, Yes? Please say that so it is on the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, yes, it was served on the Chamber and the OTP in order to enable for everyone to follow. This is General Praljak's statement. I'm just coming to that, or I was just come to that when you asked me this question. When his time was limited, we decided to try not to cause any trouble, in terms of document handling, and there has been a lot of that in this trial. I didn't particularly wish to separate the topics that I set aside in order to do them myself and raise them with General Praljak. My learned friend is now informing me that the OTP was given the binder on Friday. Therefore, I'm using this same binder to ask all these questions, because if we had physically separated my questions and his questions, it might have made it more difficult for others to follow and we might have ended up with a mountain of documents to deal with. Nevertheless, I will always call the tab number for the reasoning following. General Praljak, for the most part, is trying to follow the structure of his presentation in order to keep matters as brief as possible, but I see that he's also adding to what is presented there and his own thoughts, but he's trying to follow the logic of the structure that is already there in order to be as effective as possible.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note, could all the other microphones in the courtroom be switched off while counsel is speaking, because we can't hear counsel or anyone else, for that matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Should the Chamber understand this to mean that you will proceed to tender all documents, that is, 28 documents to be found in the binder; water, telephone, electricity, information, shelling of Mostar, Old Bridge, siege of Mostar, sniper fire, et cetera, all these other topics in the document. Are you going to file a motion in writing, possibly, to seek to tender the 28 documents, knowing that you told us that Mr. Praljak read at least half of them and that he did not have the time to read the others because he lacked time? If he had three hours, he would have read document number 1, entitled "Water," or document number 2, entitled "Telephone," et cetera?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Your question foreshadows what we hoped we might be able to do. It was for the sake of efficiency and in order to aid the Judges and the OTP that we tried to use this entire binder, tabs 1 through 28, after completing our questions on these matters, in order to tender it, for ease of reading, and then you can judge its probative value. That is up to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, we got the message. Yes, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Just forward record, Mr. President, the Prosecution is going to object to these written texts being tendered into evidence or being accepted. The general gave his opening statement yesterday within the time-frame set by the Trial Chamber. He's now a witness in the box. He's taken the solemn declaration. Witnesses don't come to the Tribunal are read pre-prepared statements and then tender those speeches or written statements into evidence. The evidence are the words that come from his mouth, in my submission, Mr. President, and so I don't -- I don't want to take more time on it, but I think there is a distinction between what the general says and then what is contained in these pre-prepared written texts that they're proposing to tender. And so it's our position that the written texts are not admissible, but that's for another day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Trial Chamber will deliberate on this topic. We note your position. We note Mr. Kovacic's position. Very well. Continue, please, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic, I have a question. Mr. Praljak dealt with the topic of destruction of buildings in Mostar by the JNA or the Republika Srpska. He told us that he asked for the destruction to be filmed. He has a film, he has a copy of it, and so has the Croatian Television. Did you plan to show us the video? Because this could be evidence that what is alleged in the indictment -- in the indictment, it is alleged to have been destroyed by the HVO, but that in fact it was destroyed by the JNA or the Republika Srpska? Are you going to show this to us or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I do have the material. It's over an hour long. I was convinced that the book "Urbicide," authored together by Muslims and Croats, describing with a great degree of precision the destruction, might be better evidence backing my claims than the film. But if you want me to, I could show the footage as well, the Svenko [phoen] house taken from an angle above the house and then swinging down. It's really dead boring and it might take some time. If you really want me to, I can show you that, maybe a small portion of the material, maybe everything. It depends on how much time you have. But I was convinced that the book "Urbicide" and the two or three exhibitions in Paris and in Zagreb and everything that would present clear and unambiguous evidence as to who destroyed the Mostar bridge, the Old Bridge in Mostar. That is my position, but then it is up to my lawyers to judge that, and we can also attach the tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I could just add a single sentence to what Mr. Praljak has said. We conferred with our client, and we decided to apply the principle of best possible evidence. We considered this subject, and as Mr. Praljak said, the best possible evidence would be his book "Urbicide" prepared by an independent commission, a mixed commission, if you like. We have heard witnesses who spoke about how the book came into existence. The chief editor was here talking about that, as a matter of fact. That is why we believe that the other piece of evidence was of lesser value, as General Praljak said. But if you want to know about that specifically, no problem. It is somewhat boring. It takes a long time to see the whole thing. We can show you the whole thing. We can show you an abridged version, but we have not included it in the 65ter.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear the last part of counsel's answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have in front of you Judges that are going to rule on matters, and you said something that I don't agree with. You said that the probative value of the movie is less than the document. I don't agree, because a book or a document can have been just made up; but something that has been filmed, that was filmed then by a party, whatever party it was, that's something visual, unless of course they were edited; but that has a higher probative value than what may have been written in a book or was a photograph, because the weight of a picture, in my book, is greater than what someone may say because you can see precisely what happened. So the reason why I'm saying this is also because I refer to something I can say in open session. I refer to the decision of the ICJ in the case Serbia and Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, in which there is a large part devoted to destruction in Mostar, and I noted that in that part of the decision of the ICJ decision, there seems to be mention of buildings that are mentioned in our indictment for facts that are attributed to the HVO; hence, the interest in seeing and watching this film. The footage was taken at the time, if I understood Mr. Praljak properly, before HVO fire, of which he claims that it was only focused on the boulevard separating the front-lines, and having no other objectives.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, no objection to raise about what you said. I fully agree. What I said was merely an assessment that we made. We tried to think about the simplest way -- the best way to present evidence, backed by live witnesses. That seemed the most practical course of action to take. Obviously, we welcome your suggestion, and we shall be more than glad, especially as concerns Mostar 1992. We might be getting to that over the next couple of days, and we might have the footage ready by such time. I do have to consider the form. Will we present the entire footage, or maybe just sections, or maybe we shall give the whole thing to everyone and then they can pick whichever sections they are most interested in, but we have absolutely no reason to hold back anything that's in our possession.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If the film is one hour long, of course, you're not going to use one hour out of your time, because you don't have all the time in the world, but you could maybe select five or ten minutes, the most relevant part.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you, Your Honour. I think we know the general direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: General Praljak, I think you wanted to add something about this.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm just trying to say that I prepared this and I wrote it under oath. I am here asserting that I wrote here is true. I wrote this on my own, unaided. I also assert that the translation that was produced in Zagreb was produced for that purpose alone, just to hurry things along over the three hours that I hoped I would be allotted. So that's that. I further assert that in Eastern Mostar, after the clashes between the HVO and the BH Army or, rather, the attacks by the BH Army on the HVO, the Command of the 4th Corps was in the centre of town. The Command of the 1st Motorised Brigade of the BH Army was in the centre of town. The Command of the Military Police was in the centre of town. The mess of the BH Army, their kitchen, was in the centre of town. The ammunition storage units they had, the depots and everything, was in the centre of town, and the military commands, finally, were in the centre of East Mostar. Further, I assert that the BH Army soldiers and civilians were mingling on a regular basis. It was all mixed up, and they were bringing weapons in all the time. This was something that was easy enough to observe on a daily basis. In those conditions of war, obviously, many people were wearing uniforms that weren't, strictly speaking, supposed to be wearing uniforms, and there were children carrying weapons through and through. What the International War of Law has to say about that, well, you probably know more than I do. It is the right and duty of a military commander to destroy any enemy military targets. It is necessary to use a proportionate number of artillery shells for that purpose. The word "proportionate" is interpreted as the amount necessary to destroy or disable, for example, an enemy bridge, enemy communications, enemy HQ, and so on and so forth. I assert that the HVO commanders, headed by me, abided by that right and that duty, or rather had we done that, the number of artillery shells fired on the area of East Mostar would have been at least 1.000 times greater than the number counted by the members of SpaBat, even without taking into account the artillery shells of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you. You used, in your answer now, and I quote the word, quote, "proportionate" is termed as "the amount necessary to destroy or disable, for example, an enemy bridge, enemy communications, enemy headquarters, and so on and so forth." Now, I would only like to underline that you misunderstood the meaning of "proportionate." Of course, I do not have before me now the text of the -- I mean the articles of the given Geneva and The Hague Protocols and Conventions, but I am sure that the proportionate is referring to the fact that the very aim of the -- to destroy a certain building or whatever should be proportionate with the results of the efforts -- the military efforts that is being employed by the parties concerned, that is, one or the other party in the armed conflict. So, therefore, it is not about the question of the ammunition, et cetera, but it is a question of being proportionate with the very aim of how to complete a military operation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Judge Prandler. I tried to find an exact definition of the word "proportionate." Nevertheless, it is still about the putting of action, something that is targeted, unless we take into account such countries usually considered to be the best representatives of international law, such as the United States. For example, they attacked Serbia, and disproportionately they destroyed over 60 bridges [as interpreted] of the TV buildings. Proportionate, that's what it means, according to their doctrine, put out of action a military target as defined by military law to keep it from continuing to operate. Lawyers, of course, give the definition a wide berth at times. They try to avoid defining exact balance this means. "Proportionate" means putting out of action, putting out of operation. All these things were in the town itself, and according to standard charts, thousands and thousands of shells more would have been necessary to put all these out of action. All the witnesses we've heard here agreed on one thing as to the number of shells. The HVO commanders fell far short of taking full advantage of their right, despite the fact that their mortars were next to the hospital. Some of them were mounted on cars and were used to fire throughout the town. Despite all of this, the smallest possible number of shells under my command was fired, and those shells were fired on military targets, and nothing else but military targets. I'm claiming that. There is both proof in the military charts that I attached, but finally it will be up to you to judge the meaning of this expression, "proportionate," under the terms of the Law of War. And then I believe we can study other examples from the wars waging throughout the world right now at this moment by the great powers. I think that should be a reference point that we should all abide by and decide and define our own concepts in relation to. Thank you very much. I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, I think it's time to move on to our next topic, that being the Old Bridge. I would like to point out one more thing to the Trial Chamber and to everyone else in the courtroom. General Praljak will provide no more than a set of brief reference points in relation to this topic, which is a topic that has been dealt with already. We might have to return to that subject, but I hope there will be no further need for that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Please move on, General.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assert that at the time, I commanded the operation of crossing from the right-hand riverbank to the left-hand riverbank, these HVO units involved, and there were some Muslim units helping, the second day or the second night of the attack, and there was a guard set up around the Old Bridge, no more than 150 or 200 metres away from the Serb lines. I gave orders to the HVO logistics to build a cage around the bridge to protect the bridge. Several lorries were needed. Thick planks to protect the bridge, seven centimetres thick, to protect the whole structure. It was mortar shells raining down, for the most part, and we wanted to keep those from inflicting further damage on the Old Bridge because it had been damaged very much already. So those planks that were wrapped around the Old Bridge were supposed to absorb these detonations by these mortar shells, shrapnel flying throughout the area, without causing further damage to the bridge. That's why I did that. There were a total of between 30 and 40 young men involved in this, and as they went about their tasks, they were facing grave danger. They were in danger of a single shell or two shells killing 10, 12, or even 15 of them in one foul swoop.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: May I request counsel or the witness indicate what's the time-frame that he's talking about. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, when you provide this type of information, please provide dates, because when we write the judgement, we will have to put dates to confirm or dismiss what you said. So you said that you gave orders, but when did you give orders, in which month, on which day? Well, it might be difficult to tell us the day, as such. But I'm also surprised, Mr. Praljak. I looked at the three binders, and in them I could not find any military order you would have signed. For instance, you said here that you gave an order. Was it an oral order? Of course, if it was an oral order, it has less value than a written order. And if you wrote an order, it must be found somewhere, and then you have to produce it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, from what I know, verbal orders have the same weight as the written orders in a war. When an operation is launched, it is impossible to issue written orders; some minor ones, yes. However, verbal orders are given during an ongoing operation. So this was a verbal order, and people who were engaged in the task, some four or five, signed a statement which will be submitted to the Trial Chamber as to who had given them the order and what they did and when they did it. It was in the month of June 1992, two days after the beginning of the attack that started on the 14th of June, 1992, at 5.00 in the morning, or 4.00 or 5.00 in the morning. So not the first night, the 14th; it was between the 15th and the 16th of June, if my memory serves me properly. I am a bit confused at the moment, but that was the time. It was then when 30 to 40 lads obeyed my verbal order, and you will see their statements, protected the Old Bridge by way of tube construction and planks. I also claim that at that moment, as far as our attack is concerned, that bridge did not have any significant military purpose, and I also claim that I don't know which commander of an organised army would have exposed the lives of 30 or 40 men at the time when intense and heavy fighting was going on. In some armies, it would be characterized as an irresponsible act on the part of a commander, which was me at the time, exposing people to excessive danger. Also, I found justification for that order of mine in the symbolic and culturalogical [as interpreted] meaning of the Old Bridge for the citizens of the city of Mostar, because that bridge was a symbol more than anything else. I would not have protected any other bridge in the same way, I would not have saved any other bridge in the same way. Only the Old Bridge enjoyed that right because its significance surpassed any other bridge's significance. That's why I undertook all the measures. I issued that order which, in military terms, could not have been justified or reasonable, in military terms. Likewise, I assert that at the time of attacks by the BiH Army in the month of May, and especially after the end of June 1993, and throughout the time that I'm going to demonstrate clearly as the major operation Neretva 1993 which started in Bugojno and ended sometime in the second half of the month of October 1993, I assert that the HVO commanders of the operative zone and the brigade commanders, and the artillery subordinated to them, had received clear instructions from me not to fire at civilian targets or the military targets that the BH Army chose to locate among the civilian population. The Old Bridge was never targeted by the HVO, and I also assert that it was -- if it had been targeted from Hum Hill, it would have sufficed three shells in one minute to destroy the Old Bridge. All it took was three shells, the bridge was shelled, such shells could penetrate the bridge, and where its statics -- where the [indiscernible] bridge would have collapsed. Throughout the whole time of my command down there, the bridge was never targeted. Throughout all that time, it was a military target that we could see in some of the footages that were made at the time, and it was also confirmed by Muslim witnesses. If that bridge -- that bridge was a military target. Soldiers crossed it carrying weapons and ammunition for the parts and positions of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina which were on the right bank of the River Neretva. In other words, based on that and based on what I understood as being implied by the law, I was entitled to destroy the bridge. All the law provides for something else. There is a provision according to which a commander of a division which would be equal to a commander of [indiscernible], the commander of an operative zone, I or somebody else would have had the discretionary right to destroy such a facility if that facility signified a major value for the enemy side. I didn't do any such thing. None of that was ever done. There have been words about how the bridge was destroyed. I, unfortunately, cannot say who destroyed it, who did it. It will always remain a mystery, although I believe that it was a very dirty game according to what I know and one person participated in that, known by his nickname Scott, Ed Scott, who was a member of the British Army, and immediately before the bridge was destroyed he had placed his camera there, and so on and so forth. I know one thing with a great degree of reliability. Not a single member of the HVO participated in the destruction of the Old Bridge. Who was it who, on the 8th of November, 1993, shelled the Old Bridge from a tank which is visible in the footage? I don't know to this very day. The investigation started, some people were reported, and then the whole thing came to a halt and never was resumed, for a simple reason; the Goebbels propaganda found a culprit in Slobodan Praljak. Slobodan Praljak is a scapegoat who protected the bridge throughout the war in every possible way when he was commander and later on when he was no longer commander. By the way, the bridge was destroyed on the 9th of November, 1993, at 1030 hours, and as from 7.45, I was no longer the commander of the Main Staff from the HVO. I was already close to Zagreb when I heard about the destruction of the Old Bridge. So much about that. However, the Judges had in front of them some experts, the book that I wrote as well, and I did that in my relentless struggle to counter the harangue of lies and smears and defend myself and say that I had nothing to do with the destruction of the bridge. The contrary is true. I protected the bridge, I saved it, and on the 8th, when I had been formally been dissolved of the duties of commander and I had the document in my hand, a tank opened fire. However, my powers are too small to investigate, and nobody else gives a toss about what really happened. But I will not be taking the blame for it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, let me ask the Registrar to move to private session for a few minutes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in public session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: General Praljak, I believe that this is enough and that we have managed to synthesise the topic of the Old Bridge, and now I would kindly ask you to say to the Trial Chamber what your position is based on what you know about the encirclement of Mostar as qualified in the Indictment.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: A town or a territory considers itself besieged when it is surrounded in an unbroken line by soldiers of the opposing enemy side or allied enemy forces. Until the 9th of May, 1993, the HVO and the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina together held the lines facing the Army of Republika Srpska on the Herzegovinian battle-field from Konjic to Stolac and Neum or, rather, what remained of unoccupied Konjic to Stolac and Neum. On the 9th of May, the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina attacked the HVO in Mostar, and after the situation calmed down very quickly and the cease-fire was fine, the separation line remained in the town of Mostar, the way we saw it along the boulevard, and outside of Mostar to the north and the south. The units of the HVO and the BH Army kept their positions facing the Army of Republika Srpska. On the 30th of June, 1993, the BiH Army, or to be more precise the Muslims in the ranks of the HVO, attacked and disarmed the Croatian Defence Council and its soldiers on the joint lines of defence, and from that day on the line of conflict between the HVO and the BiH Army went from the north towards the South mainly along the River Neretva, all the way down to Blagaj. And now could I be allowed to show Your Honours -- everybody has a map. Do I need to show them or are you going to look at them in your binders?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, it's up to you to decide how you will present your evidence in the framework of the time you were allotted. If you believe this is useful, do it, proceed. I'm always in favour of being shown things.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask for the map to be put on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the usher please assist the witness with putting the map on the ELMO. The ERN number is IC549. It has already been admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is not the first map. I am going to be showing them a sequence. Look at the map, please, everybody. This is the distribution or, rather, the deployment at the moment when the conflict started. The red line depicts the Army of Republika Srpska. Down there is the 2nd Brigade of the HVO, the 3rd Brigade of the HVO, and problems arose in Mostar that I've already mentioned. That's that. And after that, I would like to show --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, Mr. Praljak. The number is IC00596 is the one that you're showing right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, we've just seen a chart, a map. On these maps, could you tell us what is the date where we see the position of these armies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It bears the date 9 May, 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So May 9, 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I make a personal observation, but no one has to follow me, of course, but I look at this map and in the center I see Mostar. Mostar is encircled by the VRS, by the 2nd Brigade of the HVO on the top, the 3rd Brigade of the HVO on the bottom. Is that how we're supposed to read this map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then please explain.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On this map, Your Honours, you can see what we heard about here, and that is that there were small conflicts or skirmishes in the town somewhere around the boulevard. However, the 3rd Brigade of the HVO was composed of Croats and Muslims, and it was holding positions facing the Army of Republika Srpska, so nothing was encircled. The 2nd HVO Brigade was also made up of Croats and Muslims, and it was holding the positions facing the Army of Republika Srpska once again. The Bosnia-Herzegovina brigade, 1st Brigade, also held a position here. You see the 2nd Brigade, where their positions end, and then this continues with the 1st BH Brigade holding the position facing the Army of Republika Srpska. Then in Mostar, there were no positions until the 9th of May, but there were just skirmishes going on. So there was no encirclement, no siege, and that was the situation before the 9th of May, before the lines were to be taken up in the town itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Since the map is on the ELMO, would you indicate what you're talking about on the ELMO so we can see it there?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 2nd HVO Brigade was here [indicates]. Then we have the 1st BH Army Brigade facing the Serbian Army and the 3rd Brigade, and their units were not deployed here before the 9th of May. So the Command of the 1st Brigade was located here [indicates], and on the west side in Vranica we have the 4th Corps Command, and the very fact that the 4th Corps Command was so deep into the west tells us that the HVO had no intention of attacking anyone, because no normal commander would allow his 4th Corps to have a command deep in some territory that it wished to take control of. So this is the situation prior to the 9th of May, 1993, and there is no siege, no encirclement, quite simply joint positions manned by the BH Army and HVO facing the Army of Republika Srpska. Now, I'd like to make a remark here. In the 2nd and 3rd HVO Brigades, there were large numbers of Muslims, and we've already seen that from the tables that were shown here. Our next map is the one that the Prosecutor showed, and we have the lines there drawn in, the HVO lines - that's Blagaj - and the HVO lines go to the left of Blagaj, as you can see them. The lines of Republika Srpska take a different direction. Now, on the Prosecution map, we can already see that Mostar was not a town under siege. It had not been encircled. First of all, we had nothing to do with the Army of Republika Srpska. We were simply holding our lines north-south as the military situation developed, whereas the whole northern part of Mostar across Bijelo Polje and Bjela Bridge towards Jablanica was still open, and that's the map that's compiled by the Prosecution. And then we have another map that I compiled.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, before we look at the next map, let's have an IC number for the Prosecution map, given that we received the explanation. So may we have an IC number for that, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, for the map of July 1993 OTP, do we have a number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that map shall be given Exhibit IC1004. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Go ahead, General, please.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, we used Google for this map, and everything is very clear here. The red is the Army of Republika Srpska. The BH Army holds its positions facing the Army of Republika Srpska. The HVO had its lines along the Neretva River valley and holds the west bank of Mostar and an area under BH Army control along the very embankment. And to that map, we can add another one, so may we have an IC number for this first map, please, before I move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This Google map, could you tell us what is the date that refer to the lines that you drew?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's the situation after the 30th of June, 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you like -- you want a number for this map extracted from Google; right? Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Google map shall be given Exhibit IC1005. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This shows that the BH Army was holding positions facing the HVO and that the whole area to the north of Mostar was open. And it is true and correct that there's a mountain here, but it's also true and correct that the main line -- main road goes through Bijelo Polje towards Jablanica and that this entire area, together with Bjela Bridge, was under BH Army control. The other lane of the Bjela Bridge was destroyed in October 1993, and it's difficult to understand the reasons for that. Perhaps they were afraid that after their futile offensive, they would not be able to reach Neum and Ploce or the western borders. And after Neretva -- the offensive Neretva-93 proved abortive, they lost the battle and then citizens from Eastern Mostar would start moving to the north, they feared. So according to the information that I had at the time and that I learned afterwards, they wanted to destroy Bjela Bridge to show the people that they had nowhere to flee and had to stay where they were, regardless of the danger you face, and that you face perhaps death, too, which is contrary to international war law. And may I have an IC number for that map?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, Mr. Praljak. Could you give us again the exact date at which these positions --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... after the 30th of June, 1993. It's the same map, but I just show the HVO positions or, rather, positions facing the HVO. And the other map showed positions facing the Army of Republika Srpska. This map focuses on the north. The other map, the first map, focuses on the south.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, thanks. If I understood you well, the green line represented the BH positions, and if I'm not mistaken, the positions of the BiH and the HVO go through Mostar and separate into Mostar -- East Mostar and West through the boulevard; is that it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not through East Mostar. They pass through the Neretva River valley up until the Sarinski [phoen] Bridge and then move right into Mostar West, going down Santiceva Street, down the boulevard, down Donja Mahala, to where they were according to that very good map we saw earlier on, and then down the Neretva River valley further on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Therefore, if the BiH wants to move into Mostar East, according to this map that we have here, they could go through the mountains in the north and then just go along the VRS lines that are in red. So actually you're telling us that Mostar was not encircled. I'm just trying to understand what you're telling us and make sense of it with this map, because as you drew this map, and this is what you told us and I want you to confirm this, you are actually say that there is a possibility to access Mostar East through -- coming from the sector held by the BiH if you go through the mountains; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not only across the mountains, Your Honour. You could use the normal road from Mostar to Jablanica. You could follow that road. And I claim that they took the journalists across the mountains for propaganda reasons. Even when the bridge wasn't in existence, there was a Macadam road running over several hundred metres and you could pass by that way. So that's the first point. Secondly, Your Honours, we had nothing to do with the Army of Republika Srpska. We had our positions facing the BH Army, and it was the BH Army attacking us, so that's what these lines show. We were under siege, there was a siege, a line around a town, either joint forces -- but we had nothing to do with the Army of Republika Srpska. The fact that the BH Army put itself in a position whereby it had two fronts and two enemies, that was its choice. That's what it chose to do. And as I have shown in some of the books that I wrote, they purchased weapons from the Army of Republika Srpska and launched their operations against us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In terms of military technique, that's important, because the indictment alleges that Mostar was encircled. You challenge this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Completely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you challenge this. But from the purely military point of view, could any BH Army unit enter East Mostar going through the mountains or through another route? Was it feasible, without having to undergo HVO fire or without it being impossible to enter East Mostar because the position would have been held by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From the documents that we have presented here, you were able to see that from the direction of Sarajevo and Central Bosnia, from Jablanica, we had Zuka coming into Mostar, and with the Neretva Operation 93, they brought in reinforcements, they brought in weapons and ammunition, and that an operation which according to what Sefer Halilovic said, which was the first large-scale military operation undertaken by the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina over an area of 200 kilometres of the front from Uskoplje to South Mostar, they brought in two or three corps and had a complete artillery force and infantry force and deployed their units. And I'm going to prove that and show you that beyond a shadow of a doubt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's have an IC number for the last map, Registrar, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, the last map shall be given Exhibit IC1006. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's break now. It's quarter to 4.00. Let's break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court is back in session. Please proceed, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I think that General Praljak wanted to discuss the following map, and that is 0047 [as interpreted], the IC number, 00427.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Shall I put it on the ELMO? Perhaps it will be easier that way. I've already shown this map. These are the attack operations launched by the BH Army [indicates], and they were known as Neretva -- under the name Neretva-93, and these operations, as we've already said many times before, they began with the -- well, they began in Konjic after the fall of Bugojno, when there was a fierce attack from the direction of Uskoplje towards Rama, and then the whole line flared up. And then they made a breakthrough, both in the south around Blagaj, at around the 13th of August, 1993, that was, and then later on breakthroughs towards Hum Hill. And we read excerpts from the commander of Sector South. What was his name? Anyway, I'll be coming back to that later on. And they came to this area which you can't see on this map, but it's to within 12 kilometres of Siroki Brijeg, they broke their way through in the direction of Vrde and there was very heavy fighting in that area for several months, actually 2.5 months. So the BH Army, according to clear-cut stands, from what the commander said and the chief of the Main Staff of the BH Army Sefer Halilovic said and Rasim Delic, it was quite clear -- or, rather, they explained these operations in detail, very clearly, so I need not say any more about them, just to say that they described what they wanted to achieve, what kind of operation they launched, what their object was, and how it all ended, what the outcome was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Now, if there are no questions, I'd like to move on to the next area which in the binder is topic number 9, and the title is "Snipers in Mostar." General, I'm sure you can tell us a great deal about that. It is topic number 8, not 9, "Snipers in Mostar" then, and I'm sure you can tell us about that because you were there, you saw what was going on, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are various definitions of snipers, but in the military sense it's quite clear that a sniper is every military rifle with optic sights, which are used to draw the target closer –- the lenses are used to see the target clearly. Now, in professional armies, you choose a sniper from thousands of candidates, one or two men. Have you to take into account the humidity of the air, the speed of the wind and so on 18 for a sniper -- for a sharpshooter to be effective when targeting his target. Now, in the area, various observers referred to all kinds of shooting as sniper fire, and so there was a general area in Mostar that was referred to that way, and I claim that the examples put forward by the Prosecutor here, which I challenged, I claim that the 13 cases here could have been wounded in every other way, but not in the way the expert witness testified about. That is absolutely incorrect. I won't challenge the fact that some soldiers did have rifles with optic sights, but I will deny the fact that I or any of my commanders in any way whatsoever not only did not issue an order, but every time, in every conversation, they banned any shooting where civilians were concerned, in the direction of civilians. I cannot exclude all possibilities that -- more possibility that in a town that was divided, where you had residential buildings, high-rises and so on, I cannot say that some unknown person could have shot someone, but what I do claim is this: From all the photographs that I showed you, in view of the configuration of the terrain and the lines of the HVO, there were very few possibilities -- there were very few areas from which this could be done. Of course, the positions that were described by the expert witness in South Mostar or up there on that building in the center of town where he claims the shooting came from, it wasn't possible to hit people who were described in those cases. That's my first point. Secondly, never, during the conflict between the BH Army and the HVO, did I ever receive information from anyone about the existence of any sniper nest whatsoever. Now, the fact that people sitting in APCs heard shooting and then said that they were fired at by snipers, that goes against the grain of logic, because if you're in an APC, you can't hear very much, and if you hear shooting, you can't say where the shooting came from or what calibre was used, especially as you can use silencers or not silencers when shooting, but the bullets have the same sound whether you're shooting from a weapon with an optic sight or not. So you can't differentiate between the sound of bullets coming from those weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We might as well move on to our next topic. This is language, the Croatian language in Bosnia and Herzegovina. The indictment proposes a special theory on this. What have you got to say on this, General?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. I think this was something that Heidegger said that language was the house of being. Or, I don’t know, that at the beginning was the word, as stated in the Bible. Language is the very essence of human existence or survival. There is one thing that I would like to tell the Chamber. Back in the days when we were young, in our area there was some people who were deaf and dumb. They were dumb because they were deaf, but for that reason, especially in rural areas, almost without exception, they were also retarded. Why? Because the human brain cannot shape itself if there is no communication. The child, for example, is deaf. That must be diagnosed at an early age and there must be communication that is established with this child in another way in order to develop the child's brain potential and for the child to become a fully rational human being. Many examples are known, and if you look at any psychology textbook, will you come across a great many of those. Many examples are described where a child, for example, grew up with a she-wolf or a chimpanzee. Even in those conditions, the child will make it or will survive, even though it will be retarded and will not live past the age of 30. Even the animal screams and the language of anthropoid wolves is sufficient to stimulate a minimum brain activity which then provides for survival. If a child is left with no communication, even with the best possible care, no communication would leave a child to die. And this is also something you can find in those textbooks, because the child would not develop the ability for its brain to govern the biological functions of the body, once these functions outgrow the early instincts. All of this tells us that the brain can be structured only through language, and that is why every nation sees language as the very foundation of its existence. Likewise, we have many descriptions of prisons and gulags, the French Guiana, for example, where the people suffered, and the horrible conditions for 30 or 40 years.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. With all respect, Mr. Praljak, you're talking as an expert, and you're here as a witness. This is nothing that you have observed. That's something that you have learned, and we have also learned it, and we have also thoughts about it and could say things about it. You're asked to speak about facts that have some relevance to this case, and not to language in general. There is no allegation that anyone was deprived of language.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would just like to refer to a Chamber ruling dated the 21st of April, 2009, in the Perisic trial. I won't take up any time for this or go into any detail. I'll just quote the title. [In English] "... for Prosecution witness Miodrag Starcevic." [Interpretation] The decision is public, and I'll just read a single sentence from paragraph 11, the last sentence, quoting the Karemera case: [In English] "Factual witnesses can also express opinions, so long as they emanate from personal experience." [Interpretation] I think as soon as we've seen the general's CV, it becomes clear that he can talk about this from his own experience, given his education, given his knowledge, given his qualifications. I think he's perfectly qualified to talk about the subject. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I strongly disagree. This is a different case you're talking about. We want to hear things that are in some way related to the indictment, and so far what Mr. Praljak has said about language has no connection to the indictment at all. So please, Mr. Praljak, limit yourself to speaking about what is of some relevance to this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Kovacic. Mr. Praljak, I do share my colleague's view. I've just read your filing on English. It's under tab 9. It is indeed interesting, but this does not respond to the indictment. In the indictment, it is alleged that there was Croatisation in Herzegovina through education schools, et cetera. That is interesting. The accused should tell us, No, that did not happen as alleged in the indictment by the Prosecutor, and you can provide examples. We've heard witnesses on this already. It would be much more useful for you and more interesting to do that than to go into a theory on language that we are aware of. Of course, any human being has a language, but that was not alleged in the indictment. You are accused or charged, together with the other accused, with setting up in Herceg-Bosna an entire system through which you Croatisised [as interpreted] the language. Of course, you can meet the allegation by providing examples because the Trial Chamber will have to rule on that, saying yes, or no, or it happened not as alleged by the Prosecutor but as said by you; but you have to provide evidence for that, whilst now we are in a very general realm that does not further your case. You may say that now, but the Trial Chamber together, all the Judges, wanted to tell you that right now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand. I understand, Your Honours. I was just trying to point out the importance for a people of something like this. It is the French of all peoples who are famous for being fond of their language. I don't understand, in the indictment, what is suggested by the phrase "the Croatisation of language." To speak Croatian is no Croatisation. Croats speak Croatian. Serbs speak Serbian. In France, they use French, don't they? You can't Croatise someone as something. At the time, the official language in Bosnia-Herzegovina was Serbo- Croatian. It's that simple. The Croats did not agree to that. I, myself, don't agree. I have never agreed to Serbo-Croatian language. There is no such thing as Serbo-Croatian. It's tantamount to glossing over and trying to eradicate my own national identity. This is an artificial language that was created in order to create a super-nationalist institute which was in the service of a very harmful policy. I can't put it any other way. So there's this aggressor speaking Serbo-Croatian attacking a state, destroying a state, killing its people. In a situation like that, to expect us to speak Serbo-Croatian is a contradiction in terms. It is an irrational statement or assertion. I won't speak Serbo-Croatian. I will speak Croatian. I have every right to speak Croatian. I'm not saying that the French should not be speaking French, that the Serbs should not be speaking Serbian, or indeed that the Bosniaks or the Muslims should not be speaking Bosniak, which by the way at the time they did not even call that. Now, the Prosecutor claims that they felt in some way offended. What does that mean, to feel offended? If I assert the right to speak my own language, in my own language, causing someone else an offence, this is a dangerous theory. What I state here is that, needless to say, the Germans felt harmed by the Jews, so they killed 6 million Jews. What does it mean, feeling harmed or offended? The law does not recognise the felling of offence or harm. If you feel offended because I speak Croatian in Croatia and not French, then I am entirely at a loss. That is how I was trying to show how important language is. We used our own money in those schools, and I'm saying "we," it's not just me, it's "we," at the time when we were supposed to speak -- well, just imagine this. You have French schools in World War II, and imagine someone had introduced Germano-French as the language of instruction in these schools, and some people wanted to speak French but they saw those people as violating the national feelings of Germans or a third person actually has no language to call their own. The Bosniaks were free to speak in their own language. They were free to be taught in their own language, in peril, especially where the subjects involved a call for that sort of thing, such as, for example, their literature, their language, I would stand for that, I would fight for that. I did then, and I still would. I don't want to see my rights jeopardised, but I don't want another's feelings to put my own rights at risk. That is the essence of the problem. You see, the indictment, what the OTP wrote there, the Croats in Tuzla and in Zenica spoke Serbo-Croat, and they went to the front-lines, getting themselves killed while fighting people who were speaking the Serbian language. You really must have some very horrible feelings in order to claim anything like that. It is an unquestionable and inviolable right of people to speak their own language. They have no right to challenge anyone else's right to use their own language. Your Honours, you know all the examples. I won't be listing them. You know the Quebec example, the French language in Switzerland. There were three languages being spoken. Your Honour Judge Trechsel can choose his language, the language in which he will express himself, and no one may feel any offence about it.
