utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: You're making a lecture. We do not need your lecturing. We would like to know about the facts. Do you have any facts by which you will refute the indictment's position or not? If not, then we can go on forward. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honour Judge Prandler, I did refute these assertions in the indictment. The Croats never imposed the Croatian language on anyone. They didn't stand in the way of Radio Mostar the way people spoke. The Muslim speaker was using whichever language he preferred to use. I offered incontrovertible evidence about the way the schools were organised by the Republic of Croatia. There was teaching there in the Bosnian language before the Bosniaks themselves ended up calling their own language the Bosnian language. There were those experimental schools in Croatia. All this was bankrolled by the Republic of Croatia, and writers were part of the syllabus in those schools that wrote in the Bosnian language. All the grammar had not been written up by this point. I'm not trying to lecture anyone. All I'm saying is it's entirely counter-intuitive, absurd, to have a right like that, an inalienable right defined as Croatisation in the indictment. I don't understand what the word means, and there is not a single living soul in the world who can convince me that is actually means anything at all. Croatisation, what does that mean? What language were we supposed to be speaking? Serbo-Croatian? All right, I will stop right there. I will speak in Serbo-Croatian in a war in which I am being killed and massacred? I refused, before the war, whenever I could. When I wrote, I wrote in the Croatian language. Therefore, this is crystal clear. I'm not going to be giving a lecture on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, we spent a lot of hours on this issue. Unfortunately, I do not have before me the Constitution, but your lawyer might help me on that one, but I believe that in the Constitution of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina - this is from memory - there was a provision that gave every constitutive nation, the Serbs, the Croats, the Muslims, the right, the possibility of using their own language. Had these events not occurred, how would you have settled the language problem? You were a general in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and you were supposed to use your own language, but the other general, who would have been a Muslim, let's say General Halilovic, he was going to answer to you in his language. How can you settle that issue? Or in order to understand each other, are you going to both use Serbo-Croat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the essence of the language is not understanding. Unfortunately, we can't -- for example, there is a much smaller difference between Swedish and Norwegian than between Croatian and Serbian. Obviously, I have a dictionary of both Croatian and Serbian, here in all differences between the language in a grammatical sense and in terms of syntax, there are major differences. Understanding is just part of what a language is about. I read the Cyrillic script as well as I read the Latin script. I know Serbian literature better than most Serbs. That is completely undisputed, and I understand the Serbian language. The Bosnian Constitution did not say that each people should use their own language because the prescription was for the language to be called either Serbo-Croatian or Croat or Serbian. Needless to say, General Pasalic wrote in any language he chose. I understood that, and I would never raise any objection about that, him choosing a language in which he wrote. There is no doubt about that. No objections were ever raised, and every time there was communication between us, orders coming and going, we always understood all of that. All I'm talking about here is a name, a simple name. This is a fundamental right, a fundamental right for someone to call his or her own language by a chosen name. At the time, the Muslims, who later called themselves the Bosniaks, had no name for their language, as simple as that. Yet, until they found one, they wanted us to refer to that language as Serbo-Croatian or Croat or Serbian. Before the war, during the war, I believed and I still believe that no claims can be made for anyone to do anything like that. Later, they said that their language would now be called Bosniak, and they had every right to be taught the Bosniak language, but all we wanted was this: When we wrote something, and even nowadays that is the way it is in Bosnia-Herzegovina, all of the documents must be written up in three languages. I'm not sure if that applies in Switzerland, or in Canada, or wherever, but that's what it was like over there. Unfortunately, this is not practiced, the principal being there are more of us than of you, you don't understand the language. That would entail a great expense to use up so much paper. Let's not change the grammar or the syntax. Let's just leave it as it is, because this is widely understood. I consider that to be unacceptable, and I would never, never settle for that. It was difficult for me to even settle for this, for the name of the language being used as it is here in the Tribunal, the three names, and I stand by my position. It is simply not possible for someone to include in the indictment the following statement: that anyone can be harmed by anything like this, that we banned anyone from speaking whatever they chose. They published newspapers and magazines, and that's something that has been shown here, and they have their own radio in which they spoke in their own language. We tried to ban that. We impose anything in that sense, or anyone else, that would have been defined as Croatisation and that would have constituted a violated of someone else's right, but as far as I know, the HVO, no civilian, no military structure authority -- the thought had never occurred to anyone at all, not even occurred to anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Counsel, I apologise for the interruption. Mr. President, if I could just have a few brief words. For the last 12 to 15 minutes, I think, in our submission, the general has actually addressed himself to the issue of language as it relates to the indictment. He didn't begin that way, and that was noted by the President some time ago. The problem is that, the way we understand the time is being kept, this last 15 minutes or so is probably not going on the Defence time, and it's for the Trial Chamber to decide whether or not it should, but I think just during the short time begun today and yesterday, what's emerging is General Praljak is giving extremely long answers, addressing himself very much towards comments and questions of the Trial Chamber, and if we continue to keep time in the way that we are up to this point, we will never finish this direct examination. We're running at about a nine-week pace for the direct examination at this point, because we're getting about an hour or less of time. And I don't know what the answer is. It may be that the time given responding to the Trial Chamber's questions should be included. I don't know, and I'm sure counsel would have his own position on that, but it seems to me that the pattern that's emerging is one that is not going to work within any remotely reasonable time-frame for this direct examination to be concluded.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would not like to address this at any great length; maybe just one sentence in response to my learned friend's words, although there was no concrete proposal; there was just criticism to the effect that the system that we are applying, saying that the system is not the best and the most desirable. However, in this courtroom, you, Your Honours, particularly, you cannot consider any changes in the rules of the game that you, yourselves, prescribed at the very outset, before the game even started. I believe that I don't have to provide any further explanation as to how absurd this would be. Once the rules are set, then the participants in the game should abide by the rules, unless they are changed, of course. However, rules are never changed in the middle of a game. And this is all for me on that topic. Unfortunately, there was an intervention even before that, and I would like to answer His Honour Judge Antonetti. It is true that there is a document in e-court under 1D10236, which is the Constitution of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. You remembered the document well, and we're talking about Article 4 of the Constitution. And it is true what Mr. Praljak is saying, and that is that that article envisages Serbo-Croatian and Croat and Serbian as two official languages in Bosnia, and the Ikavian dialect as the way the languages are pronounced. The Croatian variant would be the Ikavian variant. Let's not expand the subject of language any further. No, I don't have anything else to add. Thank you very much. And the number that is being suggested to me, let me just repeat the number. [In English] If I may just repeat the number --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: -- for the transcript, 1D01236.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. I think the Chamber must react to what Mr. Stringer has brought forward. I do not envisage, and I'm sure that my colleagues agree, any change in rules, but we have to distinguish two things. One is questions asked by Judges, and they are time which is not counted towards the Defence. Another thing is Judges recalling the witness that he is to speak as a witness and not as an expert or something else. And then if he continues, of course that is not answering a question by the Judges, but it is continuing of his testimony. I think that is completely in conformity with the rules, and I even seem to realise that you also agree with this interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I absolutely agree, Your Honour. However, there is a problem there. Who will be the arbiter of that? Who's going to take the role of judge in such a case? Are you prepared to take the stopwatch in your hand, and every time the accused opens his mouth, you say, Stop, and say to the representative of the Registry, Up to here, this is us, and from there it is them? I am exaggerating, Your Honours. I'm sure you understand that, but this would take us too far. The rules are what they are. However, if you are of the opinion that the accused is going too far, you have all the prerogatives to stop the situation at that moment, as you did just a moment ago, and you have the right to warn the accused and to stop him sometime. It may be premature, because an introduction serves to open an issue, and sometimes it's not. The however, this is the way the cookie crumbles in the courtroom, and since you have opened the issue, I strongly object to any modification of the rules that exist. You can always control every speaker in the courtroom at every moment. You can tell me or anybody else, This is enough. Sit down and shut up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm happy to state and to see that we are in agreement, Mr. Kovacic, and I even agree that there may be delicate questions, but I think as a rule we can trust our Registrar, who does a wonderful job on this. We will perhaps have to control it, and you too, and in case that the suspicion comes up that there are problems, then we could take it up again. But I think it's premature now to see more problems than are actually at issue, and I think we can continue now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With all due respect, Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic, let me cut to the chase. My colleague, my fellow Judge, was absolutely right to mention all this, and I fully agree with him, but you just said something. In Article 4 of the Constitution, it is recognised that the citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina can use the two languages, either Serbo-Croat or Croatian-Serb, and if I understood you right, the Ikavian language, which means that in Mostar as well as in Herzegovina, anyone, according to the Constitution of the BiH, had the possibility of speaking Croat, the Croatian language. Is this what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not under the Constitution. This should have been the same language, one and the same, in two different forms. In schools where there was a majority Serb representation, then the teaching would be in the Serbian, and in Siroki Brijeg and Grude, the teaching would be in Croatian. There was no possibility to do it legally without being subject to punishment. It was not possible for a teacher to say, for example, to children, Children, you're now going to be taught Croatian. That was not even possible in Croatia proper. The term used there was "Croatian literally language," a language used by novelists and writers. I started talking about the problem of Croatian language on account of which people ended up in war started from the declaration on the Croatian literary language that was written in the 1970s by intellectuals who were against unification. I reduced my speech to a minimum. You cannot know things. I don't want to pretend that I'm an expert, but I know a thing or two about the language. At the moment when an aggression started, the people that were exposed to the aggression could not speak or use the language of the aggressor. They had their own language where they called Croatian, and when that was introduced into school and when that was being used, then it was the beginning of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, Mr. Praljak. Let's not spend too much time on this. Your answer to the question, of course this time is not deducted from your time, but my question was of a legal nature. This is what I wanted to know: With respect to the Constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina, was it possible for Croats in Mostar to speak another language than that provided for in the Constitution? That's all. You said, No. Perfect, you answered. Mr. Kovacic, please resume.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I just wanted to add to this, since the document has been mentioned under 1D01236, Article 4, we're talking about the Constitution, that we should bear in mind that that Constitution was passed by the Presidency of the former Bosnia-Herzegovina on the 24th of February, 1993. Even then, when the war was raging, what was being done was a copying of the Constitution norm that existed during the existence of the former Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia. Maybe I should ask the General just one more question since we've been talking about the language at such great length.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: General, you mentioned on several occasions that the Bosnian language did not exist at the time. Do you maybe remember when the first reference of a Bosnian language was made at public gatherings or professional gatherings or when the term started becoming used at any significant rate?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a long, long time ago, but I would not go into that because that would --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, General.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a fellow citizen of the honourable Judge Prandler, Kalaj, who was the governor of Bosnia-Herzegovina, who tried to invent the Bosnian language, but that was connected with the annexation of Bosnia-Herzegovina to Austro-Hungary, and it is a broad area. But the essence of the matter is this: You lawyers should agree whether the Presidency could pass the Constitution, which Presidency could pass the Constitution, which Presidency can pass a Constitution? The Bosnian language. The Bosnian language that was first introduced into the territorial schools for the children who were Bosniaks and Muslims in the Republic of Croatia in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- because I believe in order to give them the right to use their own language as a people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I believe that we have explained things very well. If there are no further questions, I would like to move on to the next topic, which is number 10 in this binder, and it is the issue of presidential transcripts. A lot has been said in this courtroom about that. We've seen a lot of them also. You have your position on that, General. Can you please tell us something about that? Can you tell us what you know about the presidential transcripts?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Although the integral reading of the text which we call presidential transcripts does not reveal anything mean dishonourable politically unacceptable unless some people stirring and insisting on their ideas. However, these conversations were taped secretly, and the participants did not know that they were being taped. To my question, this was testified by the Prosecution Witness Manolic. Second of all, what was said was abbreviated from the transcription from speech into text. There was the possibility and it did happen that there was a wrong match between the person who said a certain word and the text attached to that person. For example, I would be ascribed the words of Mr. Karnavas, Mr. Karnavas would be ascribed the words of somebody else. This is because people spoke without introducing themselves. I would, for example, say something, and I did not precede my words by saying, This is Praljak speaking, and then the words who transcribed had to speculate who it was, whether it was Praljak, Karnavas, Kovacic, or whoever. Number 2, Franjo Tudjman, the president of the state, did that in his office because he was a historian, and he hoped that he would live longer, and he wanted to use the documents for his historical synthesis. The transcripts arrived at a court, in my layman terms, in a legally invalid way pursuant to a private decision on the part of President Mesic who gave the transcripts to the journalists and told him, Do whatever you want to do with them. Furthermore, speech within a family, speech in closed session, speech at free seminars, of free universities, speech in editorial rooms in newspapers, speech at closed sessions of judges, are all speeches that imply the freedom of speech as a thesis, as a possibility, and sometimes this is contrary -- what is said is contrary to what the person really believes. This is examining all the possibilities, speech as a possible provocation, speech as a gain. That is what is done at universities. This is a freedom which doesn't imply that what is said is necessarily what you actually mean, that it reflects your position. It has never been so. I'm going to skip the theories of the language by Saussure and Chomsky. I'm going to skip all that. However, when such a text which was transcribed and cannot be authorised in the spoken utters, the words are often accompanied by gestures, laughter, even a sarcasm; there is grovelling up to somebody, there is acted anger, and when all this is reduced to the essence, what we arrive at is a text that may mean absolutely different from what is actually said. I remember at a session -- at a meeting, Gojko Susak had just returned from Canada, and they always would use their fingers to show that something is being quoted, that something is in inverted commas [indicates], and, for example, he would say that Nika was an excellent chef yesterday, and then he would show with his hands that her dinner was not actually good, whereas in the text what you would read was that Nika was an excellent chef and that she prepared a very good dinner. That's why I'm saying that if the raw text would reflect the possibility of what the essence of the speech was, there would be no theatre, you wouldn't be able to have Moliere’s The Miser, or Don Juan, or Hamlet or King Lear. They could only be played in one and only way. That's why the actors play,that's why the directors direct. They take the raw text and they produce those texts in hundreds of different plays, giving the words multiple meanings, and that's without any further adieu when it comes to me to explain what I actually said and what I meant at such meetings. I would like to say that you cannot transcripts -- you cannot judge the transcripts in such a way, especially not the details there of. In my layman's opinion, I don't think that this can be a piece of evidence in any trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: General, when we're talking about transcripts, I believe that two questions would be in order. You have looked at a lot of these transcripts; if no others, then at least those that the Prosecutor has submitted. Just say "yes" or "no." Did you find, in any of the so-called presidential transcripts, at the beginning of such a transcript as is customary in our lands, that there is a clause that the minutes from the last session are being adopted? Have you ever seen that in any of the transcripts?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. General, you also mentioned recording. Is it true that there was audio-recording in most of the situations and that there was no video-recording at the same time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have absolutely no idea. I never saw videotapes. I never saw anyone videotaping me or audiotaping me. And nobody ever told me that I was being filmed or recorded, and nobody ever offered up any text for authorisation. Now, I know what authorisation means, when you give a statement for the press and then you authorise it. And I have an example with respect to an error, a mistake. Well, if you want to ask me about that, but not at the expense of my time; that is to say, how mistakes are made when you convey somebody's words without putting them into context.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Well, one more question, and we'll come to that when we look at the individual transcripts, but let me ask you this now: Do you know that there is no longer any original audiotapes from the sessions, that they don't exist anymore?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'm going to object, Mr. President. The question is a leading question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I admit, I admit. I admit that it is misleading, but it is a notorious fact in Croatia, so every day newspapers --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: That's an even greater reason not to allowing leading questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Okay. I think that I don't have to rephrase question, because Mr. Praljak is smart enough to provide --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Finish your answer, Mr. Praljak, with just one sentence, if you would.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I won't be led. I don't know that, but from relatively reliable sources, from a friend of my son's, Miroslav Tudjman, Tudjman's son, that tapes were erased, so there weren't enough tapes and things were erased and taped over. So that's what I know about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, I note a contradiction in what you've just said. Earlier, when your counsel asked you why all this was taped, you said a couple of things. You said that you didn't know, that these were secret tapes, but you also added, to justify the taping of the conversations, that Mr. Tudjman was a historian and that for history he wanted to put all this on record. But this being the case, and of course one can understand Mr. Tudjman's approach, if he wants to keep all this for the record for history, he's going to make sure that everything said will be recorded for historians, for later -- for the future, and he wants to make sure that everything is absolutely faithful to what was actually said. And now you're just telling us that according to Mr. Tudjman's son, who is a professor - there's many professors, but there's another professor that we're learning about - so according to this new professor, he said that they were erased -- that they were erased, so there's a contradiction. So why would Mr. Tudjman want to keep a record for history while, at the same time, erasing the tapes as they are recorded? Do you have an explanation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I said all this on an assumption, because Miroslav Tudjman doesn't know exactly whether these tapes were erased or not. This is something he heard about later on or had to surmise. It's his conjecture. According to what he said, it was erased, but it's not contradictory for the following reasons. At that point in time, we -- well, the president -- we weren't a rich country. Of course, tapes are not very expensive, but we didn't use the small cassette tapes. It was the larger tapes that were used on a professional tape-recorder, the Nagra or whatever, to ensure that sound was good. It's those tapes that were expensive, and he probably wanted to have things written down. Now, I'm just guessing here, but I know that you can't look at it as if you had a French budget to spend. There was very little money for everything. There was a shortage of money in every area, because there was a war on. Later on, I will present the data about the unemployed, about how much the army cost.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is a bit surprising. You might be right. I don't know. But if I compare this to what we know of East Germany, where citizens' conversations were taped, and in the archives all these wire-taps were kept, I assume that in Croatia there were also wire-tapped conversations that were kept, and I guess in the BH also there were wire-tapped telephone conversations that were kept. So if you keep these kind of records, why not keep the transcripts of high-level meetings between Mr. Tudjman, his ministers, and eminent political personalities? Why erase all that? I really don't understand this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I did not claim that I know any of this for certain. I don't know how much tapping there was. I do know how much there was in the former Yugoslavia, but one thing I know for sure. On Croatian Television, for example, and it filmed under wartime conditions at the time, tapes were erased, the ordinary better-type tapes. Very important material was erased because there simply wasn't enough money to buy new tapes with, and I know that for a fact. And, among other things, the Kodak negative that I mentioned earlier on that I had received and sent to Mostar, I received it from Germany through my private channels, and at the time this cost several thousand marks. It was a great deal of money at the time, and you couldn't get that money easily. It wasn't readily available. So what I'm saying about television, I say that with every certainty. As to the rest, I can't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we didn't think it was necessary to put exhibits of that type on the 65 ter list. But in the Kordic and Cerkez trial, the Court was shown statements by three witnesses as to the circumstances of how the audiotapes were used, how they were transcribed, how the tapes were erased, and then finally how the electronic records on the computer were erased. So I say with full responsibility, on the basis of exhibits before this Tribunal - I'm not testifying, I'm just providing you with this information and you can look up those testimonies - that ultimately the Prosecution showed transcriptions and photocopies of transcripts of goodness knows which generation in order. That's all I want to say, and if necessary I shall ask that the exhibits and the witness statements from Kordic and Cerkez be presented here, but I don't think that will be necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Now, General, I think we can move on to the next area, which is topic number 12 in our binder, an important topic, and it is the question of the assistance of the Republic of Croatia to Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I claim that all humanitarian convoys reached their destination. All humanitarian convoys for Muslims, Croats, and for all others who lived in the non-occupied part of Bosnia-Herzegovina passed through the HZ-HB with permission. All those convoys were loaded up in one of the Croatian ports, organised by some of the 270 registered humanitarian organisations in the Republic of Croatia. And I also claim that as representatives of these humanitarian organisations, and I know this for a fact personally, that through the -- through Croatia and the HZ-HB, some 5.000 fighters from Islamic countries and also from Western countries and Westerners converted to Islam, passed through that way, and all of them entered with regular international passes of humanitarian workers. And I also claim that nobody in those areas were ever hungry. They never went hungry, except for people in Sarajevo for some of the time. And I also claim that weapons were smuggled, as was food, medicines whose validity had expired. There was narcotics smuggling, cigarette smuggling, and alcohol. Hazardous waste was deposited. And all this led to the disapproval of the fighters and the occasional unauthorised stopping of the convoys. Every such case was resolved and the convoy reached its destination. That is true for the eastern part of Mostar during the BiH attacks on the HVO. One of the convoys that was stopped in the attack of the 30th of June, well, there was an interruption for a time, as far as I know, but -- and there was also another interruption when the BH Army launched an all-out attack in Blagaj and the south of Mostar in 1993, and I personally several times insisted that the persons be punished who would stop a convoy, and that was quite normal in wartime conditions. And also we were quite conscious of the fact that the convoys of humanitarian aid were going to areas where there was a large population, but they also went to the BH Army. Now, in what measure, I don't know, and I don't know what the international war law says about stopping convoys intended for the enemy army, and that civilians must be separated from the army, and that the distribution of goods should be supervised. But, anyway, all the convoys did get through, they all passed through. There were rare cases in which they were interrupted, and everything came in through Croatia except for some of the aid that was dropped from planes in the Sarajevo area. So that's what I have to say on that topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Now, for the benefit of the Trial Chamber, the question of aid to -- from Croatia and so on, we'll discuss that later on.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I just add one thing?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never in the history of warfare did one people, like the Croats in this case, help another people, that is to say, the people of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and then they turned their army against the HVO, and I claim that that was along with permission from Dr. Franjo Tudjman with the knowledge of the Government of Croatia, and permission from them and from Gojko Susak and the Minister of Internal Affairs Jarnjak and with the knowledge and permission of Slobodan Praljak. Never in the history of warfare did the commander of the HVO allow a convoy of weapons to pass through to another army, the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and when that army, the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, used those weapons to attack the very people who brought those weapons in. And as far as I know, this was permitted and approved by Bruno Stojic and Milivoj Petkovic and Slobodan Praljak and Valentin Coric, and I also know that the body called the HZ-HB, or let's call it with a reservation, the government, led by Jadranko Prlic, never opposed that. And I also claim that an action of that kind against one's own people in every country anywhere in the world would have been characterized as high treason and those persons would have ended up on the gallows. What I want to tell the Judges is this, and we'll have a witness to talk about that, not only about the conflict on the 9th of May and the 10th -- 30th of June, but after the conflict as well. From the Republic of Croatia, convoys brought in weapons to the BH Army, and in Zagreb, in locations that I'm going to tell you about later on, we enabled those weapons to be packed together with tins of food, and what actually happened was that those weapons in those convoys were transported to the BH Army, that is to say, to their central base in Visoko. Now, if one of you were to give me your son and then I provide weapons to someone who's going to kill your son, you can't envisage anything more serious and graver than that, but the HVO did that. We smuggled weapons against ourselves to enable the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina to defend itself in Tuzla, in the east in Gorazde, and so on and so forth, and then quite certainly they used those same weapons and pointed them at us, they used them against us. And that's what witnesses have spoken about here. We had a witness testifying on one occasion when he was English, and we said, Yes, we gave weapons to both sides. What he meant was he provided both Chiang Kai-Shek and Mao Zedong the weapons to fight each other, mutually kill each other. But can imagine the French forces giving weapons to Germany, that never happened. It was only the leadership of Croatia and the leadership of the HZ-HB, with me at its head, that did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So much about that the humanitarian convoys and one of the forms of aid and assistance. Now, for purposes of -- well, you were speaking generally about all forms of aid from the Republic of Croatia to Bosnia-Herzegovina, so that was a general overview, but we'll take the specific instances later on in due course when we come to topic 12 in our binder.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I've already told the Judges about this. My Defence team gathered together documents relating to the aid and assistance from the Republic of Croatia to the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Muslims, and it has filled 92 binders. Those 92 binders were brought to The Hague here, and I showed you photographs of those binders, and I couldn't bring in 92 binders into the courtroom. They're all on CD-ROM and can be used. Of course, in proceedings of this kind we cannot look at all the documents in those 92 binders, and that's why I made a summary of those. And I will provide the Court with that, and it says quite precisely how many documents there are, what the documents are, and how many documents are recorded in the book that I compiled. We provided assistance in the form of weapons. We packed -- packaged those weapons in food supplies and loaded them up onto trucks, UNHCR trucks. Units were set up in -- and sent to Bosnia-Herzegovina to fight. There were training centres of the BH Army in Croatia. BH Army pilots were trained in Croatia. Logistical centres of the BH Army existed in Croatia, both in Split and Zagreb, and Rijeka too. So at a point in time when the HVO allegedly attacked and expelled and so on and so forth, together with Franjo Tudjman, as it said, at that point in time the BH Army had logistic centres to collect weapons, to receive aid and assistance, where barracks were placed at their disposal, and that's why I said that large portions of the indictment are quite absurd, and the world has never seen the likes. Humanitarian organisations on the territory of the Republic of Croatia, well, there were 270 of those, or a similar number, through the port of Ploce and Split and Rijeka. Planes brought in -- flew in assistance, aid and assistance. And I don't want to repeat everything, but, anyway, Croatia took in over half a million refugees from Bosnia-Herzegovina. Croatia organised ex-territorial education for pupils, Muslims, in their own language. They didn't call their language that at the time. Anyway, there was cooperation in the field of sport. For example, Croatia helped the sportsmen from Bosnia-Herzegovina to go to the Mediterranean Games, to attend the Mediterranean Games. So all this evidence is contained in that book, and how can anyone say that Croatia wants to cut off part of Bosnia-Herzegovina and attach it to its territory, and allows the sportsmen from that country to travel using the money of the Republic of Croatia, sportsmen who trained on Croatian training-grounds and then go to the Mediterranean Games, recognising that Bosnia-Herzegovina was a Mediterranean country, whereas it only has the small stretch around Neum, and then you call it Greater Croatia or whatever? Certainly, we wouldn't have sent the sportsmen over there, if you had plans of a different nature, whereas you lend international dignity to them and you allow them to take part in these various games. There was basketball competitions and so on and so forth. Now, assistance to Bihac. It was not possible to keep Bihac going without the efforts of the Croatian pilots and Muslim pilots. At the beginning, there were certain routes that had been broken through, and I took part in helping those young men out until some of them were killed. I helped them carry the aid and assistance. So the Republic of Croatia, when a third of its territory was occupied, when it was engaged in battle, when its economy and tourism had completely been routed, invested all-out efforts, and if anybody were to tell me that such a small country, under the given circumstances, provided somebody else the assistance that Croatia provided, if you can quote any example in history, then I'll be happy to say that I know nothing, if you are able to say and claim that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: We could say a great deal more about this, but General Praljak will be offering more information on certain specific forms of assistance at a date later on. The next subject that we shall be touching upon is tab 13 in the binder. I'm talking about what I think I shall rightly term the famous Tudjman-Milosevic meeting in Karadjordjevo.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a fairy tale, a myth cooked up by a shady agent. We shall be talking more about that, so I shall not speak about this now at any great length, but please look at the map "Greater Serbia Aspirations." I think it's right here. I will be showing all these books. I'll be showing all the evidence, thousands and thousands of pieces of evidence. It all points to one conclusion. The aspiration was to create a Yugoslavia like this [indicates], for this whole portion to be torn off. Now, the logic eludes me. How would Franjo Tudjman think of carving anything up within Bosnia-Herzegovina, dividing anything with Milosevic? Milosevic wants a country all the way up to here [indicates], that's what he's after, conditionally speaking. I'll get to speak more about that later on. There was, I think, a total of 43 meetings between the various Republican presidents after the breakup of Yugoslavia. Tudjman and Milosevic met a total of 43 times at these meetings and conferences. 31 times out of these 43, Alija Izetbegovic was around. There was a letter I handed over to the Chamber when they wanted to know where the letter was from, and it states clearly Franjo, you will be meeting Milosevic. I heard -- mind you, it says that I heard that he will table a proposal for carving up Bosnia-Herzegovina to you. So the Secret Service and everybody else, they had organised themselves already, released this about rumour to the effect that Franjo would be carving something up. It was a rumour that was circulated in a bid to prevent the two statesmen from reaching any sort of helpful agreement. How was it possible to carve up Bosnia-Herzegovina, and which part of Bosnia and Herzegovina should have been annexed by Croatia. I don't know. As the honourable Judge said, I did have a role to play there. It wasn't a major role, but it was an important role, yet I never had an inkling of anything like that, not in my wildest dreams. Nevertheless, this was a myth perpetrated by powerful secret services with certain powerful players involved. The myth is perpetuated ad nauseam, and then everyone involved, and I will be presenting some very specific arguments about this at a later stage, they were all saying that this was entirely pointless and meaningless, that this was nonsense, and then the most important thing, can you please tell me what the consequences were of that agreement, all of the aid that we have seen here in Croatia shipped to B and H, Tudjman's desire to sign an agreement? And, Your Honours, you will see that as early as 1991, Franjo Tudjman put an offer on the table to create a joint army, joint armed forces. This was a proposal he tabled to Alija Izetbegovic through his then high-ranking official Hamed Filipovic, and he wrote it down in his own memoirs. This is all a bundle of lies and speculations that have nothing whatsoever to do with reality. In case you're interested, Josip Pecaric, an important mathematician, I've got something about that here. He's one of the two most important mathematicians as far as equations are concerned. And he said, All right, this man, Milosevic, he must be insane. He had the tanks, he had the cannons, and Tudjman had nothing at all. He had a handful of rifles, rifles bought from Hungary for the police, and there were people who bought some weapons on their own. And Milosevic comes up to him, with all the military might at his disposal, and he says, Okay, let's do a brotherly deal, 50:50, and carve it up. All right. This is totally counter-intuitive, if you ask me. This is a meaningless topic, scandalously stupid, and yet it is perpetuated on and on like that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, I wanted to deal with this later, but since you have just spoken about the division and you said it was stupid, I listened to you and I looked at the map. Unless I'm mistaken, I believe that part of Croatia had inhabitants of Serbian origin. If there had been a division, as was said by the Prosecutor, how do you think -- the issue of Serbs in Croatia, how would that have been settled?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I mean, Your Honour, you see, first of all no -- nobody knows how they carved it up or where. All right, I'll show it right here. Most of the Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina lived around Banja Luka and then to the east, that entire area, most of them. And then there's the Muslim enclave around Bihac. The Muslims were there. And then further up, across Croatia's border, there were certain areas with some Serbs living there. In terms of percentage, not too many, really. It was the smallest group of Serbs. Most of the Croatian Serbs lived in Zagreb. Nevertheless, this was a traditionally poor area, and territorially speaking, this is what was termed the Krajina. All of the rest was occupied by the Serbs. How should I show that --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: General, I think you should simply stand up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [In English] Your Honour, even better, you got those on A3 format maps, and maybe we can do that after the break. You can have the map, and Praljak will explain this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the time has come to have a break, but Mr. Praljak, you fail to answer my question. I started on the hypothesis that Tudjman and Milosevic divided for themselves Bosnia and Herzegovina. Let us assume that the project existed based on such a project. Here's my question: How would the issue of Serbs in Krajina be settled? Would Tudjman have to accept that the Krajina would go over to Belgrade, and therefore that his territory would be diminished, reduced? How could this have been done?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honour, that is precisely what I'm telling you. I have no idea. It defeats all logic. It's entirely counter-intuitive. Franjo Tudjman never -- and maybe not even then would have yielded a single inch of Croatia's territory without the necessity of military defeat; nor would I have. I would have fought on until I fell down. This is beyond all doubt, and it's also beyond all reason, I'm afraid. But there's something else, too. If someone wants to have --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note, the interpreters can't hear Mr. Praljak because he's too far away from the microphones.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me. They're saying that they can't hear the general because he's not close to the microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Could not the map be transplanted a bit to the right, seen from us, so that it is practically behind Mr. Praljak, and we can see him and the map at the same time?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is a little bit difficult with moving the map, and there is another one on the other side, so maybe we should do it after the break, we should prepare it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's have the break now, and all these logistical problems can be solved then. Let's break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Praljak will respond to your question. The point is only he can use the big map behind him or, alternatively, you have got these A3 format maps, and he has one, so whatever will be more convenient.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'll start out with the assumption suggested to me by Judge Antonetti. I will try to pursue this logic of a possible division. It would be necessary to know some history, but I'll skip that. At any rate, back when the stories began even before the war, the Serbs, because they were what they were in Yugoslavia, believed that this part of Croatia [indicates] was territory that belonged to them, the area surrounding Okucani and what was later termed Western Slavonia. They also believed this territory to be theirs, the Banija territory south of Karlovac. They also believed Lika to be theirs, this area here [indicates], and then the Velebit hinterland, what we normally called Zagora, the area around Knin, and then all the way down to the sea coast. Obviously, they believe Zadar was theirs too, but we'll come to that later, and they took these areas eventually. In Bosnia-Herzegovina, they believed Banja Luka was theirs, Mount Kozara, Grmic, around these parts, and all these, all the way down to Livanjsko Polje, Bosansko Grahovo, Bosanski Petrovac and Drvar [phoen]. In a way, it was part of their historical consciousness. They believed these areas to belong to them. Even back in World War II they committed heinous crimes against the Muslims. We have had a witness here who spoke about that, but I will later show what sort of casualties were involved and what sort of massacres were committed along the Drina Valley against the Muslims, precisely because their objective was to somehow break up the Muslim ethnos here in this part of Pestar Plateau in Serbia [indicates] because Sandzak contains a large Muslim minority. Eastern Herzegovina in their eyes was entirely theirs. No reservations whatsoever: Nevesinje, Trebinje, Gacko, and so on and so forth. Probably they believed Eastern Slavonia to be theirs. They destroyed Vukovar, they laid it to waste, and so on and so forth. So even if they gave up the plan about the Karlobag-Virovitica line all the way up here, I don't know about that, except they offered Franjo Tudjman something like this: Here's a country, it looks like this, but what about the Muslims in that case? The Muslims would then yield all of this to the Croats in a country looking like that. Your Honours, I really don't know. I don't know of a single Croat -- I'm not talking about Franjo Tudjman. I don't know of anyone who, in their wildest dreams, would think up something like that. This is entirely absurd. It is entirely counter-intuitive, like nothing else on earth, and that's how the situation evolved. That's as far as they went, because we stopped them right there. I, myself, stopped them south of Sisak, north of Sunja, when I was still fighting in Croatia, and so their plans fell through, and I simply can't bring myself to understand, and I don't know if anyone does. What part of Bosnia-Herzegovina are we talking about, in addition to all these parts of Croatia they thought were theirs, in the sense of Serbs living in those areas and it had to be Serbia Yugoslavia, Yugoslavia, Greater Serbia under the guise of Yugoslavia. No other assumption is feasible. It would have been an impossible task to carve it up like that, and the logic doesn't work, even if we assume all these things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: General Praljak, please slow down. You are trying to say too many things all at once. The map in front of the Chamber is 3D03545. I believe there will be other opportunities to use that map. Therefore, let's keep it close at hand. General Praljak, we are now coming to the next meeting mentioned in this trial. I'm talking about tab 14 in the binder, for the reasons following. I'm talking about the Boban-Karadzic meeting that took place in Graz. Just for the sake of the record, we have had P00187 admitted into evidence, the 6th of May, 1992 meeting. What can you tell us about that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We've heard witnesses here -- well, one of them was actually at this meeting, and all I'm trying to say is the following: Under the assumption that something was agreed at this meeting between Boban and Karadzic, some sort of a cease-fire or something like that, here's what happened after the meeting: There was a large-scale attack by the Army of Republika Srpska on Livno, a large-scale one. Following this meeting, the HVO liberated Stolac. Following this meeting, the HVO liberated, after the Serbs had previously expelled nearly the entire population of East Mostar on the 15th of May, 1992, and made them cross to the west bank. People were jumping into the river. There were some casualties at the bridge, and so on and so forth. So after that, the Croatian Defence Council liberated not just the western bank but also the east. It attacked the VRS and the JNA and scored an impressive success, thereby establishing the lines that we looked at. There was another attack in Rama. After that, the Serb forces attacked and took Jajce. After this meeting, there was incessant fierce fighting around Bosanska Posavina up here [indicates]. If I could just use this one, I have the map, but I'm trying to use this one. That's it. So following this meeting, the Serbs attacked Livno, expelling from the east bank in Mostar all of the people there to the west bank. The HVO, that is, we, took Stolac. We liberated the hills on the right-hand riverbank, the right-hand riverbank in Mostar, and we reached the right-hand riverbank. Several days after that, the HVO crossed the Neretva and liberated Mostar in all this area here around Bijelo Polje and all that. The Serbs then attacked Jajce and eventually took Jajce. There was another attack at Rama, one which failed. There it is [indicating]. Throughout this time, of course, following the fall of Jajce, the Serb forces stopped short of Travnik. I was involved in that. I will be talking about that as will my witnesses, of course. After that meeting, there was fierce fighting in Posavina, in Bosnia-Herzegovina that went on for months. Eventually, the Posavina area was lost and the River Sava was reached, with the exception of a small section along the river. Now, what was this meeting about and what was agreed after the meeting? Yes, and, yes, there is something I forgot, the Operation Bura, another operation that we addressed, which occurred in October or November of 1992. I think we tried and were to some degree successful in showing the Serbs how we could take territory or at least that it was a show of force; therefore, they gave up any further substantial attacks to us throughout this area. That is as much as I can tell you about that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We may be needing this map at a later stage. Can it be assigned a C number, please, in case we plan on using it later on?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, the map shall be assigned Exhibit IC1007. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There you go. Your Honours, now that I'm at it, can I just say that what we see marked here are the positions of the HVO, and it's over and beyond what is suggested in the indictment about some Banovina or something. The HVO units were established anywhere in Bosnia and Herzegovina where there were any soldiers -- rather, any Croats at all. They were established as armed units defending Bosnia and Herzegovina. The positions marked here are only those units that were outside the purported Banovina. Needless to say, the question that I might ask is: Why should one establish units outside this territory to be defended, territory to be purportedly annexed to Croatia? Who will they be fighting? Who will they be defending from, or who will they be defending against someone else? There is no inherent logic in that, but it's not my inference to draw. There's another map that I have on the ELMO. This is Operation Bura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, Mr. Praljak. Let us return to the previous map. You have just spoken about the Banovina. Let's look at the deployment of the HVO brigades, the 7th -- the 107, 108, 110, 111, et cetera. We've got red lines on this map. That's the way the Serbian forces were positioned; is that right? We've got two red strokes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So militarily speaking, this famous, quote/unquote, "Banovina" was surrounded by Serbs; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You see, Your Honours, Bihac is not in Banovina. We have our units. Sarajevo is not Banovina. We have our unit there. All of these units that have nothing to do with Banovina apart from this one unit in Posavina, in part, in part. There were many more there, many, many more. An army made up of Croats and Muslims, and there is no logical link between that and Usora, Gradacac and Tuzla. These units, they have nothing to do with Banovina. We don't have the map now, but the Banovina is about this part, around Neretva, Stolac, and so on and so forth. The best part is there and there is a small part that is about here. All of these units were set up in an area that had nothing to do with the so-called Banovina. These units had more soldiers than me, than the soldiers I had available to me. The HVO numbered a total of about 40.000 soldiers, no more than that, or thereabouts. Fewer than 20.000 were actually available in this area conditionally named the Banovina. More or less all the rest were under the command of the BH Army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: May I just ask a question still about this map. Perhaps I missed something, but what is the time that is depicted? At what time did this situation prevail?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the situation as it was, roughly speaking, back in 1992, before the Posavina area fell. This is the situation or the months that followed the talks between Karadzic and Boban. It remained like that from the beginning to the end, except where we lost our positions, and then the units from Posavina, with the exception of some who remained there to defend some sectors went under the command of the Tuzla Corps of the BH Army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Another map, Operation Bura, the 8th of November, 1992. Again, the HVO put together some forces -- assembled some forces with the assistance of the BH Army, insofar as it was developed at the time, and then it attacked the units of the VRS in the way displayed here. One cannot say that the operation was completely successful or that we had managed to ship the lines forward in any major way. One thing is certain, though. We inflicted large-scale casualties on them, and this was a show of force -- a sufficient show of force, in fact, to dissuade them from attempting anything in the Neretva River valley. It was a convincing show of force, and it told the Serbs one thing; that we were a powerful army, and they would not be able to get on with their ways as they had earlier on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: General, following this explanation, and I think we have a clear picture now, if my understanding's correct, please answer with "yes" or "no." All of these events that you've just described, does this picture not deny the possibility of an alleged agreement between Boban and Karadzic in Graz?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: That's a leading question, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is what I would like to say. If there is any logic at all, then this should constitute a denial of any putative [Realtime transcript read in error "punitive"] agreement. If there is no logic involved, then we can say whatever we like. There is another thing I would like to say. Unfortunately, I missed that earlier on, but if the honourable Judges look at what I have provided, there is one unit from Olovo. We forgot to mark it on the map. I tracked it down later on. I knew that there was a unit in Olovo. If you look at these pages here, you can see that. The BH Army, fighting alongside the HVO. The name of the unit was Matija Divkovic. Another unit of the HVO that we failed or forgot to mark on this map that I offered. Olovo is far away from the Banovina area and it simply doesn't make sense to place it in that context.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Just an observation on the transcript. On page 83, line 24, we read "punitive agreement." Probably it should be "putative agreement" or something of that kind. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You have addressed a number of chapters in this binder. I would now like to move on to tab 22. You wanted to skip some portions, and then you skipped this one because you wanted to keep it brief, 22. Would you just like to say something about this? The title is "Peoples Right to Self-Determination." Is there something you would like to say about this, even briefly, something to add?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll try to be very brief and not take up too much time with this. Just the following. I assert, and I have proof of that here, that James Baker, in his statement, the one that is attached here, clearly backed the preservation of Yugoslavia as a whole. He thereby gave a green light to the JNA to move ahead. He declared Slovenia and Croatia to be separatist countries. Given the context of that statement made by such a high-ranking representative of the United States, it was interpreted to mean, We are against separatism, and you, gentlemen, it down to you to resolve the situation by weapons, of course, and that's how the war was triggered. And I'm saying this peacefully. This is strikingly amoral. I find it stunning and terrifying. We had no weapons. We didn't even have the TO weapons. All we had was endless bravery, the endless bravery of our lads, but we still managed to survive and preserve our country. And then the Security Council imposed an embargo on weapons. I am saying this calmly and peacefully. I cannot imagine a more scandalous or amoral or more miserable decision. It was a decision that was made against the rights of individuals of nations to self-determination, which is a right proclaimed in international law. It is also the violation of the right to self-defence. It causes nausea, such as the one I read about in Jean Paul Sartre's book. It's very difficult to be in trenches when they pound away at you with mortars, planes, artillery weapons, and you have nothing. You only have the trenches, and maybe you have a handful of rifles to respond, but no more than that. What followed after that was this: Croatian citizens, citizens, much more than the army at that point in time, laid siege to the JNA barracks in Croatia containing lots of weapons. Some of the barracks were taken. Varazdin, for example, was teeming with weapons and equipment, but then, and I know this for sure, Croatia was forced, in order to not keep evoking the Serbs, to allow the weapons to leave for Bosnia-Herzegovina, no less. The weapons for Slovenia left for Bosnia-Herzegovina, no less. This was probably done in a bid to convince us that they would be using the weapons to plant flowers once it came to Bosnia-Herzegovina. It is hard to imagine a form of political blindness worse than this. What happened later on in Bosnia-Herzegovina, you know that all too well. Nevertheless, there's another thing here. First of all, you impose an embargo. An embargo is to be observed. That's what the law says. But if you observe the embargo, you'll end up getting yourself killed. I would have understood if the embargo had been imposed, introduced, and then one of the great powers came along and they said, No war, please, we'll protect you. You can't bring in weapons in, but we'll protect you. No one is there protecting you, and you have no right to purchase weapons because you violate that law. This is not a formula that works, as simple as that. That's how it was, the only way to get weapons was in the black market, and what I'm saying is that in a more or less secret way, the state authorities, the banks, the players in the economy, hundreds of thousands of Muslim and Croat individuals, those from the Ukraine, Slovenia, Hungary, Germany, Turkey, Iran, Argentina, France, Switzerland, all of those who wished to help, some of those just wanted to make money, of course. The embargo was violated. Anyone who was in a position to violate it did so. First of all, later on, the Americans, as Ambassador Galbraith said, turned more than a blind eye to everything that was going on simply because they had realised at one point that this was -- there was simply no moral justification for this. And then what happened was something that was even worse. Weapons were purchased in this way, and that led to the following: The state authorities in Bosnia and Herzegovina and Croatia simply compromised their position of authority. If you leave the role of purchasing weapons to people who weren't always honourable people and shady individuals, and these people purchased weapons which in turn provides them with social status, with some sort of power, people who were selling cows in order to buy weapons did not bow before the authority of an army. It belonged to him. He was the one who bought the uniform with his own money. And this applied to both Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina, and this to a large extent ruined any authority enjoyed by the state bodies in Bosnia-Herzegovina and in Croatia, to say nothing of the army. It took a long time for the shipments to become more legal than they used to be, to be placed under control, for weapons to be given to people and the process to be monitored to some extent so that order could be brought to the situation. This is something that to a very large extent at the very outset is something that continued for a long time. It was a situation where order was difficult to establish. I won't say it was a situation of disorder. He said, Well, what power of command do you have over me? It was my money, I bought the rifles, so I'll do whatever I like. And they did with the rifles whatever they like. What I want to say about these divisions, one thing I don't understand to this very day: When the Croat-Muslim offensive, following explicit orders by the Americans, stopped just short of reaching Banja Luka. We have the indictment here that we were carving up Bosnia and Herzegovina, which -- the entire Bosnia-Herzegovina, thereby creating a state where the Serbs, after everything that they had done, they get 49 percent of the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And the Bosnians and Croats get 51 percent of its territory, and the Serbs create a state called Republika Srpska. Bosnia-Herzegovina, it has no -- may I just be allowed to complete my answer, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I just wanted to ask if the general could tell us the time-frame, the date of the Croat launching the offensive that was stopped, just so we have a time-frame for all of this.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was probably an error in the transcript. General Praljak said the Croats and the Muslims together.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the Croats and the Muslims, that's right. That was in 1995, after the Operation -- Operation Storm. First of all, one operation, then Operation Storm, then the operation where the HVO liberated Kupres and reached the Livanjsko area, Livno Plateau, and came to behind the forces of the Army of Bosnian Krajina, and then an agreement was signed, a military agreement between Alija Izetbegovic and Franjo Tudjman, and the Croatian Army was legally allowed to cross over on to Bosnia-Herzegovina territory when Bihac was liberated, and they moved towards Banja Luka. This is something that Holbrooke writes in his book. Did we make a mistake or not when we stopped them there? We thought that that was the right thing to do at that time. General Gotovina was told to stop in front of Banja Luka and not go forward. They were called to Dayton afterwards, and a map was placed before them, and there was to be absolutely no discussion. 49 percent of the Serbs, 51 to the Muslims, and that was the division of Bosnia-Herzegovina that was legalised, that is in force today and is functioning today. 200.000 Croats were expelled from the area, never to return, and I am sitting here, among other things, because it is said that I started dividing up Bosnia-Herzegovina. After all the documents that I've shown you, well, tell me now, Prosecutors, where do you have -- where is there any logic in all this? Where is the logic of it all?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please. We have another mistake in the transcript. On page 88, line 23, General Praljak said that 49 percent was given to the Serbs and 51 percent to the Croats and Muslims together.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: General, now the next chapter in this binder is entitled "Indictment." On Monday, that is to say, yesterday --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before you move on to the next chapter, Mr. Praljak, you mention James Baker, and I looked, and then I went on to the following documents. And if you don't mind, let us speak about the Geneva Agreement dated 23rd of November, 1991, signed by Tudjman, Milosevic, Kadijevic and Cyrus Vance. Have you got the document? Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've got it in my binder. Please, after Baker, yes. No, this is a resolution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After the resolution.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've found it, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I've always tried to understand who was the first to start. That's the issue of the chicken or the egg. Now, there may be an answer here in this document with four points, A, B, C and D. What do we see? Under A, Croatia is required to put immediately an end to the blockade of the barracks of the JNA in Croatia. Under B, the JNA will have to withdraw from Croatia, et cetera. But it seems, in the way events unfolded, and you said that yourself, by the way, it seems that the Croats blocked the JNA barracks, and then all the other events ensued. Can you confirm what is found in this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. On the 23rd of November, 1991, in Croatia the war was already in full swing, and we had Vukovar and all the rest of it on the 23rd of November, and for several months I'd already been at war. There were lots of persons dead. We blocked the barracks, of course we did so, that they wouldn't shatter us. We blocked the barracks of the Yugoslav People's Army. When it says "people's army," it means the Croatian people, too. The Croats are people, too. But we purchased the weapons with our own money, sent to the budget. Of course, this was under great pressure, and the weaker side always has to give way. But if we had been stronger and if it had been my call, I would never have de-blocked the barracks. I would agree, of course, to having all the soldiers and officers leave and go home, but the Yugoslav People's Army was a Yugoslav Army and a peoples' army. It wasn't a Serb army so that the Serbs could control it any way they like. They took the weapons from the Territorial Defence. They had a lot of weapons in Serbia and were able to do what they liked in their barracks. These were barracks on the territory of the Republic of Croatia, under an aggression by that army, and they had to be deblocked. And had there not been such great pressure -- well, of course President Tudjman was criticised and the people were embittered, because to allow the weapons to leave and then to have them beat you in all these areas which were already occupied at the time, Your Honours, to have them kill you and you to leave weapons -- let weapons go that you had purchased yourself, was a very serious concession which emerged from weakness, not through morality, or a just cause, or whatever. And we have videos to show that all the weapons went to Bosnia-Herzegovina, where that dance macabre was to be continued. So it's not a matter of the chicken or the egg, which came first, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you very much for your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: General Praljak, for the record, you discussed the indictment and it was erroneously recorded on the transcript yesterday, page 32, line 14. It was recorded as being topic 23, but it is Chapter 23 that deals with the indictment. And what I want to ask you now is this: Well, you mentioned Chapter 24 and the statement, and I'd like to ask you now something about Chapter 25, which is titled "Simulation Based on Percentage Comparisons," the number of victims, I'd like to underline the word "simulation," and examples were taken with the number of inhabitants, the surface area of countries such as France, or the USA, comparing it to Croatia. Would you explain these slides to Their Honours?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I prepared this simulation in my introduction when you have me five hours to speak, and as far as I remember, it was Judge Antonetti who showed some interest in looking into this more fully. The number of victims is often looked at in absolute terms and no relation to the population, so in order to show you how dreadful the war was, I compiled this simulation with Croatia, which has 4 million-odd inhabitants, 189.000 expelled, 11.000 killed. I think the figures are greater now, but I think they are illustrative enough, 26.000 persons wounded; unidentified persons died, 782. Let me add to that that about 1500 soldiers of the Croatian Army are still listed as missing and their graves not found. By 2008, a little under 2.000 Croatian soldiers committed suicide. On the next map, we see France, and quite simply I looked at that in proportionate terms. And the population in Bosnia and Herzegovina, if it were to be superimposed on France, it would mean that there were 26 million Muslims, 80 million Serbs, and I've turned the French into Croats, and then there would be 10 million of those Croats or French in Bosnia-Herzegovina. There would be 4.800.000 others. On the next map, I superimpose France on Croatia. It's not quite possible, given the shape of Croatia and the shape of France, but I did this as far as it was possible, geographically, to do that. Then I went on to page 6, and I showed you what an attack against France would have looked like, the way Croatia was attacked from the territory of Serbia, Montenegro and Bosnia and Herzegovina. On page 7, I showed the French territory that would have been occupied or conquered by foreign troops. And then I come to my most important point on page 8. If we look at the number of inhabitants of France, which is 60 million, a population of 60 million in France, that the following figures would correspond, which means that about 5 million Frenchmen would have been expelled, there would be four and a half million refugees in France, 151.000 would have been killed, 351.000 wounded; unidentified persons died, 10.000. And the French soldiers, French defenders, if we stick to the ratios, should have committed suicide after the war to the tune of 26.000. So these figures -- well, Judge Antonetti is French, and the French -- this would help the French understand what the ratio of the victims and fatalities were, because if you say 50 people were killed in a town called Rama, that figure does not reflect the situation. And I devised the same sort of thing on page 10 for the number of refugees and displaced persons who were French from Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, apart from the fact that I find it a bit difficult in considering this to be evidence of a witness, it seems to be some sort of a relatively witty, perhaps, expert essay that you present to us, so this is not -- but then it is also highly polemic. If you look at page 7, you have put France in there, but you have completely changed the proportions. I must say, I find this rather criticable [sic]. France would be much bigger, in fact, if you took it. So this gives an indication that the whole thing you present here is probably not very seriously presented, and I think it would be better if you dropped it now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't agree, Your Honour. Look here, let me explain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, I'm not arguing with you. I have looked this up now on the map in Google, and France -- the size of France almost would have covered or even more than the whole of Yugoslavia, and here you put it only in a small part. This is polemical, and I think the Chamber does not want to hear this and there's no reason for the Chamber to listen to that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Trechsel, if I may -- please, I would like to respond that I did not compare France to Yugoslavia. This is not what I'm claiming.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, I must recall that your role is that of a witness. You have been sitting in this court for three years. Numerous times, you have heard the Chamber telling witnesses that they are not here to comment or to explain; they're here to answer questions when they are asked, full stop. You have chosen to posit as a witness, and this is also valid for you. Mr. Kovacic, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] However, you have not -- you do not understand me properly. I am talking about a misunderstanding. I believe that the witness has a right to point to the misunderstanding from it arises your objection. I'm not denying your right to rule this courtroom; however you said that France is bigger than Yugoslavia. Yes, it is, indeed. However, I'm talking about proportions here. I put France in the place of Croatia by way of proportioning it because in my view proportions are important, Judge Trechsel, in order to see how many people really died down there and what was the state of chaos, and how much blood was shed, and it's important for this case, and I expect from this Trial Chamber to allow me to try and explain the catastrophic consequences of this war.
