It's very important for me as a witness, as a person, for this not to be a game, not to -- for me to play the game of a spectacular expert. I am trying to compare facts, and I did it in the best of the intentions in order to explain to everybody the atrocities of war by comparing facts. I've just showed how much territory France would have lost and how many victims it would have had. I'm very calm, I'll listen to every objection of yours, I'll stick to the rules. Rest assured I'm willing to do all that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I may be of some assistance. I will attempt. I believe what General Praljak is doing is not comparing the actual sizes, but trying to put it in proportion, as he's just indicated, saying if France was the size of Croatia, and I believe the demonstration was for purposes to illustrate the psychological impact it would have had on the Croats in light of the circumstances. Given that, I believe the Trial Chamber has seen this before. Mr. Praljak has provided his explanation. I believe we can move on. I believe the point was established by General Praljak and is well understood at this point by everyone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacic, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, because there might be a discrepancy of view regarding the Judges, as far as the Judges are concerned, regarding this. Mr. Praljak, during your preliminary statement three years ago, you did mention this, you did deal with this issue, so we know all this. On page 23, we have a chart, a chart that you actually drew up, and we should all look at this chart because it will help us save time. You say in Croatia there were 11.296 persons killed, and if this was compared with other countries, like France or the USA, but you might also have used Hungary or Switzerland as examples because then there would have been no problems as far as the Bench was concerned, then we would have found out that, for example, when you compare what happened in Croatia to what could have happened in the USA, there would have been 739.000 killed, 1.7 million wounded, which is a huge number, and as far as refugees are concerned, 46 million of refugees, which illustrates the impact of what happens psychological to each and every one. I think we all got your point, and Croatia might have been a smaller country, but still with this we note the impact that these events had on each and every one. But you already told us about this earlier. We knew about this. Mr. Kovacic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like to do two things now, just forward record and for everybody's information. I would like to say that the slides and the entire simulation have been introduced into e-court as 3D01077, and that part refers to France, and the following slides and simulations refer to the US of A, 3D01078. This is just for an easy referencing. And now if you allow me, maybe Mr. Praljak would conclude the whole answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't have nothing else to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I suppose and I hope that everybody is clear that the comparison shows how it was possible to manage the situation or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, now I would like to move to topic number 26, which is human behaviour in civil unrest, or, rather, in complex situations, which include war. Again, we have a number of slides which have been produced with the intention to simplify the whole matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution objects to this line of questioning. The witness is not qualified to give opinions about this issue, nor is it, in our view, relevant to the case, although he might intend to call an expert to testify about this at some future time. We suggest it's irrelevant, the witness is not qualified, and we should move to something that is more relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would say this, if I may: First of all, General Praljak, in his biography, says that, amongst other things, he graduated with a degree in Sociology, and this is nothing but sociology. Second of all, this is the general's special field of expertise. And third of all, I'm going to refer to the decision that I've already quoted earlier today, which is the decision reached by Judge Moloto's Chamber, dated 21 April 2009. [In English] "... for Prosecution Witness Miodrag Starcevic." [Interpretation] It says very clearly in paragraph 11 thereof that, and I quote in English to be faithful to the original: [In English] " Factual witness can also express opinions so long as they emanate from personal experience." [Interpretation] I believe that personal experience in this case, based on your practice in this courtroom, also the knowledge of personal knowledge, Your Honour. In any case, when it comes to the testimony of an accused, which is a specific situation, I believe that he should be given the right to explain what he knows and what he can explain, and he can also say how he came by his knowledge. If there are any doubts about his knowledge, there's always room to ask additional questions. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, the witness has no personal knowledge. He wasn't in New Orleans when Hurricane Katrina hit. He wasn't in New York during the blackout. He wasn't in Amsterdam when Mr. Theo van Gogh was killed. He wasn't in Paris during the rioting there, and he wasn't, I don't believe, in Vietnam when the My Lai massacre occurred. Now, if the general wants to talk about issues confronting him in his capacity as commander, it's the -- the effect of the war and the civil unrest on his troops, and how it affected or did not affect their own conduct in the field, he's certainly, based on his own personal experience, well qualified and positioned to talk about that. But he doesn't have any experience on these issues, nor does he have any sort of expertise to comment on them generally, and so in our view again this is irrelevant testimony and we should simply move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: If I may, just one sentence, Your Honour. I think it was obvious, but obviously I have to say that. And excuse me, I would like to switch on Croatian. [Interpretation] It is the prime --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic, regarding this issue, as far as I'm concerned, but I believe my fellow Judges share my opinion, Hurricane Katrina, the New York blackout, the assassination of Theo van Gogh, and what happened in Paris, well, it is true that the witness was not a fact witness to all this, and we are going to waste time indeed. However, I believe that there is one topic which is perfectly relevant. It is the massacre at My Lai. Of course, he wasn't there, himself, but this case, which was actually tried, does give rise to the problem of command and control. Out of memory, I remember that this is an issue that is mentioned in a number of documents produced by the Praljak Defence team, and, Mr. Kovacic, you might ask questions to the witness on the situation that a commander might be in with its -- according to the troops that are subordinated to him to check whether they are in control or out of control, because here I agree with Mr. Stringer. But the other topics are totally irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I would like to add an observation. I'm not contradicting what the President says, that the My Lai experience may, as such, have something to do with matters that come up here. I think that will also come up in an expertise, in an expert opinion that we'll hear. But looking at what is under number 26, I am struck by the fact that in -- at the end of it, pages 33 and the following until 36, we have a reference to sources, and this is a rich documentation of sources, and this is the style exactly of an expert opinion. This is not testimony. This is an expert opinion by someone who really cannot claim to be heard in these proceedings as an expert and who, in fact, is heard as a witness and not as an expert. I think this is very clear if one looks at the papers under number 26 as a whole.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The general will, of course, serve as a fact witness as well, there's no doubt about that. However, bearing in mind the methodology of work and the possibility of drawing conclusions about facts in such a mega-trial where everything is packed in a story that spans a period from 1991 to 1995, and even later than that according to the Prosecutor, General Praljak, as the accused, was of the opinion that some terms have to be explained and put on the table for an easier understanding of the possibilities given to a commander in the war that we are talking about here. It's not difficult to start with My Lai, because it is closer in terms of the issues. However, we are talking about the sociological issues of chaos. Be it My Lai, or Hurricane Katrina, or the New York blackout, sociological rules apply and they are the same. The general has a degree in Sociology. He is an accused. He was accused a long time ago, and of course as an intellectual he was dealing with all that and did all the research in order to comprehend the possible arguments in favour of the ability to control or the inability to control an army that was established overnight. In keeping with your instruction, because I don't have any other choice, I'll ask the general to start with the example of My Lai, and if you believe that this may apply to any other chaotic situation, then we can talk about such situations as well, or maybe not. However, I would kindly ask the general to explain to everybody and to put My Lai in the context, and to see whether he, himself, found the same rules that are explained here and interpreted here from the point of view of sociology and sociological science, did he see the same things in Bosnia-Herzegovina, where he served as a commander.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All this time, it seems to me -- okay, Judge Trechsel, I understand the notion of a fact witness. However, the indictment consists of facts, but it also comprises a whole --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The general is not answering the question that his counsel put to him, he's making a speech to the Trial Chamber. We ask the witness be directed to respond to the questions that his counsel has put to him and to not address rulings already made by the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Answer the question first.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's a simple answer to the question. It is not true that, from individual crimes or particular crimes that may have happened or did not happen in a certain area, this method can be used -- the induction method can be used in order to draw conclusions about the existence of a joint criminal enterprise. This is a political and sociological thesis, it's not a legal thesis. That's why I'm saying that the example of Katrina, where there was an outage and a flood, the outage in New York, Theo van Gogh's case where mosques were set on fire, no perpetrator were found, shows a mass -- shows what is the relationship between mens rea and actus reus, and this is what the Prosecutor wants to skip, because they don't know sociology and that's why my right is to defend myself in the way that the indictment was construed. The indictment doesn't say Praljak did this or that, committed, but strangled, killed, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... yourself. You are not invited and entitled to plead your case. You have chosen to posit as a witness. As a witness, you have to truthfully and, as far as possible, even coolly answer the questions put to you, full stop, full stop, and that is the role, and I must really ask you to stick to that role. Please, Mr. Kovacic. Maybe it is good if you formulate, in a very precise way, a question which relates to -- which is a question to a witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic, please proceed. The answer is very simple. What has been done here has not been done by an expert. This was researched according to my instructions and -- for me to answer the question why things were happening down there contrary to the wishes, the acts, the commands, and so on and so forth. This is my attempt to explain in this court all the forms of a phenomenon that will lead us to the truth, and that's the long and the short of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Just a few more questions to explain all that. Do you, with these examples and this literature, do you want to show that there is a series of possibilities because of which some crimes happened in Bosnia and Herzegovina between 1991 and 1993, as the indictment alleges?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I object to the leading question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: It is not a leading question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, sir, I claim that under the conditions of such social disorders which are even less than a war, because of the nature of the human being, because of the nature of society, some acts are committed which cannot be ascribed to any intent or actus reus, and let me proceed. For example, you cannot say that the car manufacturers are to be blamed for the people who are killed in car accidents, and there is as many as 30.000 of them in America, or maybe drug manufacturers, or cigarette manufacturers, who kill millions of people, but nobody closes down such factories. In my case, my best feeling, and please don't be angry, Judge Trechsel, I'm not trying to show my --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, you are not --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm trying to answer questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: No, you're saying, My claim is that, my claim is that. I quote you from the translation. And you should say, I have seen, I have heard, I have felt, I have smelled, your personal experience. Maybe you can say, When I felt this, I felt so-and-so; or you could say, My adversary, my comrade, told me so-and-so. But instead you're giving us theories. This is all theory. It may be a correct theory, I'm not taking a stand on that, but we should try to conduct the hearing of someone as a witness the way witnesses are heard.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, Mr. Karnavas. I have something to say. The problem we have with Mr. Praljak's testimony is the following. Actually, it comes from the fact that he is a witness. The question is to know whether he should testify as all other witnesses we've had so far or whether he is entitled to go beyond a fact testimony and defend his case -- defend himself by dealing with topics that are outside what a fact witness could deal with. Few accused have testified so far in this Tribunal, only a few of them, and it always gave rise to a number of problems. I note that we have a divergence of views within the Bench. Personally speaking, I fully understand that an accused would want to testify on facts, but also want to defend himself. This is my own position, but I understand that I'm in a minority here in this Bench. Given this, the accused is here to answer the questions put to him by his counsel, and only that. He's not here to make any speculations, and he's not here to enter into guess-work, or assumptions, or whatever. He is here to answer the questions that are put to him point-blank. This is what the majority of the Trial Chamber seems to believe. I must say that personally I'm of another opinion, but I must abide by the rule of the majority. Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. And, again, this is just for the sake of trying to add some clarity or perhaps some assistance. I've been listening to the testimony quite keenly and to the objections being raised and what have you. I believe that because General Praljak also has military experience, in a sense he can be viewed as an expert. That said, however, I believe that at least at this stage of the proceedings, perhaps, there will be fewer objections, both from the Prosecution and from the Bench, if General Praljak would be descriptive from his first-hand experiences, and then perhaps down the road, if it's necessary to draw some similarities between his experiences and some other events, historical events, that may be appropriate. But for now, I think perhaps if General Praljak would stick to providing more detail as far as first-hand experience, what it was like to command, what it was like to be in a situation where soldiers were not of a trained nature, such as in other countries or what have you, and from that description then perhaps he could lay the predicate -- the factual predicate upon which then he can explore this area. But I believe maybe there's been some mis-stepping of the laying of the foundation, and that's what's causing some of the problems. And it's 7.00 right now, but perhaps -- you know, we're still early on at this stage, this is a very engaging direct examination, and I'm sure General Praljak has been listening to all of the objections. I see him smiling, and I'm sure tomorrow he will be even smoother than today. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if you'll allow me just one sentence. It seems that it might assist with this discussion. I believe that Judge Antonetti is right, in terms of General Praljak's right to testify not only about the facts, but also about his specialised knowledge, which is also corroborated by our experience from the examination of some Prosecutor's witnesses. Let me remind you that when we had military personnel, members of various forces, for example, there were UNPROFOR commanders in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, we put questions to them not only as fact witnesses, but also we put to them questions that would be more appropriate to ask from a military expert. There were objections to such questions, and the position of the Trial Chamber was as follows: One has to use all the knowledge of such persons, and if, in view of their knowledge and long experience, if such persons can help us to arrive at the truth, their testimony will only be welcome, although they don't enjoy the status of experts. I believe that General Praljak at this moment is in an absolutely similar if not the same situation, and I propose that we treat General Praljak in the same way we treated commanders who came from UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'll be very brief because of the hour. With respect to my learned friend Ms. Alaburic, the point is that there aren't any questions that are being put to this witness, really, and the witness isn't giving any real answers. What he's doing is making speeches, and it may make him feel good and it may make people elsewhere feel good, but there's no information and there's no evidence -- testimony from a witness that's taking place here. It's just speeches and statements, and that's number 1. And then secondly, Mr. President, with respect -- with all due respect, the Rules make no distinction between an accused who's a witness and other witnesses. Accuseds who testify aren't granted special status under the Rules that gives them license to make speeches or to defend themselves in any way other than answering relevant questions and tendering probative evidence through their testimony, in the same way that all the witnesses do. So to the extent -- I know there may be disagreement among the members of the Trial Chamber on this, but in our view, the Prosecution submission is that simply by taking the stand, this witness -- this accused doesn't enjoy any special status that distinguishes him from any other witness that has testified in this trial. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is five past 7.00. I think we have to put an end to the hearing. Mr. Praljak, we shall reconvene tomorrow at 2.15. We have to stop, I'm sorry, because we are now into extra time. Remember what Mr. Karnavas said, because it was very relevant. So we shall resume tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 6th day of May, 2009, at 2.15 p.m. 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25

--- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.05 p.m.,
